title: RAG foundations
subtitle: Build the mental model before choosing infrastructure.

questions.Q: What is RAG, and how does a retrieval service fit into an AI application?
questions.A: RAG means Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Before asking a language model to answer, your application finds relevant information and puts that information into the model request. The model can then explain your actual document instead of guessing from its training. A retrieval service is the part that finds and returns those passages. It does not automatically supply the chat interface, user permissions, or final answer checks.
questions.Why: First, prepare the documents for search: read them, split them into passages, and store those passages with searchable representations. Later, when a user asks a question, search for useful passages and send their text to the model together with the question. These are two different workflows. Updating the searchable document can change the next answer without changing the model weights.
questions.Risk: A search may return the wrong passage, or the model may misread the right passage. Check whether the selected source actually supports the answer. If the required rule is missing or the search service failed, report that state rather than inventing a rule.
questions.Trade: RAG supports changing information and inspectable sources, but you must operate indexing, permissions, search, context selection, and evaluation. A simple structured lookup is a better choice for an exact request status or a financial total.
questions.Try: Trace one document through ingestion and one question through search. Draw the boundary where your own generator must be called.

questions.Q: Why can an LLM sound confident while being wrong?
questions.A: A Large Language Model predicts token sequences using learned patterns. Fluent continuation and factual verification are different capabilities. If the prompt lacks the relevant fact, or includes ambiguous evidence, a plausible continuation can still be false. Confidence in the prose is not a calibrated probability that the service request is correct.
questions.Why: In the reference design, the retrieval and evidence layers supply inspectable material before a host invokes generation. an evidence-status type distinguishes missing evidence from a failed backend, giving the application a basis for abstaining or asking a follow-up question.
questions.Risk: Presenting a citation does not establish that the citation supports the attached sentence. the retrieval service preserves evidence identity, while claim-to-evidence checking and appropriate abstention remain host responsibilities.
questions.Trade: Restricting answers to supplied evidence improves auditability but can reduce coverage. Allowing general model knowledge expands coverage while weakening the promise that every answer reflects the indexed corpus.
questions.Try: Ask one answerable, one ambiguous, and one unanswerable question. Write separate expected behaviors before evaluating any generated output.

questions.Q: How are search, retrieval, and generation different responsibilities?
questions.A: Search ranks records against a query. Retrieval includes query preparation, backend selection, constraint enforcement, candidate fetching, and optional reranking. Generation turns the resulting evidence and instructions into a new answer. Treating these as one function hides whether an error came from missing data, ranking, or answer synthesis.
questions.Why: A hybrid retriever and the strategy classes orchestrate search; an evidence assembler builds a bounded evidence bundle. Their return types are useful without a chat model. This separation also supports source verification tools and ordinary search interfaces.
questions.Risk: A fallback that silently generates when search fails can convert an infrastructure outage into misinformation. Use strict retrieval and propagate backend failure into the host's response state.
questions.Trade: Explicit stages require more wiring and more status handling. They also let you benchmark retrieval independently and switch generation providers without rebuilding the corpus.
questions.Try: Design three response payloads: successful evidence, successful empty search, and backend failure. Explain which may safely reach generation.

questions.Q: When should I use RAG instead of fine-tuning or a SQL query?
questions.A: Use retrieval when answers depend on a changing collection and need source attribution. Use a structured query when the task is exact aggregation over authoritative fields. Consider fine-tuning when the persistent problem is behavior, style, or task adaptation rather than missing up-to-date facts. These approaches can be combined.
questions.Why: The retrieval service's document and evidence abstractions suit passage retrieval. A question such as total approved invoices this month should usually reach a database computation; nearest passages cannot guarantee an exact total. Fine-tuning is not implemented by this subsystem.
questions.Risk: A semantic similarity score can make an approximate answer look exact. The host must route tasks appropriately and preserve authorization on both document search and structured tools.
questions.Trade: Task routing adds complexity but avoids forcing every question through a vector index. A single retrieval path is easier to prototype and easier to misuse.
questions.Try: Classify ten realistic product questions into passage retrieval, database computation, general explanation, or behavior adaptation. Defend two borderline cases.

questions.Q: What is the difference between a document, a chunk, a vector, and evidence?
questions.A: A document is a source-level unit of text and metadata. A chunk is a searchable subdivision. An embedding vector is a numerical representation of that subdivision. Evidence is selected, attributed text prepared for a consuming model or user. These objects have different lifetimes and should not share one overloaded identity field.
questions.Why: The canonical Chunk, Document, and SearchResult dataclasses separate ingestion and search shapes; evidence types add revision, source, span, and citation information. A chunk hit becomes useful evidence only after selection and attribution.
questions.Risk: Confusing a chunk ID with a document ID breaks deletion, citation lookup, and version switching. the retrieval service carries metadata through the pipeline, but hosts must supply stable source identities and meaningful provenance.
questions.Trade: More explicit types require conversion at boundaries. They reduce accidental field loss and make changes to storage independent of the user-facing citation contract.
questions.Try: Annotate a sample result with its source ID, document ID, revision, chunk ID, text, vector dimension, and evidence label. Identify which fields can change after reindexing.

questions.Q: What do dense and sparse retrieval mean?
questions.A: Dense retrieval compares learned vectors, making semantic paraphrases discoverable. Sparse or lexical retrieval scores token-based signals, making exact names, identifiers, and unusual terms discoverable. They capture different notions of relevance. Neither should be described as understanding the user's authorization or guaranteeing truth.
questions.Why: The retrieval service separates a vector index and a lexical index capabilities and composes them in hybrid retrieval. PostgreSQL offers native full-text search; some other adapters approximate lexical ranking with token overlap. Those are different implementations, not equivalent language models.
questions.Risk: Dense retrieval can confuse related concepts; lexical retrieval can miss synonyms. Hybrid fusion reduces dependence on one signal but adds its own ranking choices and cannot recover absent source material.
questions.Trade: Two signals increase implementation and evaluation cost. A keyword-only strategy can be preferable for exact support codes or a prototype with no embedding service.
questions.Try: Create queries containing a product code, a paraphrase, and a misspelling. Predict which retrieval stage should help, then inspect both ranked lists.

questions.Q: What does grounding actually guarantee?
questions.A: Grounding means giving an answer process explicit evidence it can use. It is a relationship between a service request and supporting material, not a property conferred by vector search alone. A grounded workflow must preserve provenance, show the relevant revision, and handle insufficient evidence honestly.
questions.Why: An evidence assembler deduplicates, merges eligible spans, budgets rendered context, and creates citation labels. revision-aware source lookup can retrieve a bounded span from a retained revision. These mechanisms make verification possible rather than automatically performing every verification step.
questions.Risk: A wrong retrieved passage, stale document, or unsupported inference can survive into the answer. Host-side citation checks and evaluation are still necessary; delimiter escaping is only one mitigation against untrusted source instructions.
questions.Trade: Strong attribution needs snapshot retention and richer metadata. Minimal text-only search is cheaper but cannot support reliable historical verification.
questions.Try: Write an answer with three factual claims. Map each claim to an exact evidence span; flag any sentence whose support requires an unstated inference.

questions.Q: How do relevance, correctness, faithfulness, and freshness differ?
questions.A: Relevance asks whether material addresses the question. Correctness asks whether the service request is true. Faithfulness asks whether the answer follows the provided evidence. Freshness asks whether the evidence reflects an appropriate time or revision. An answer can be faithful to an obsolete policy and therefore be incorrect for today's user.
questions.Why: The reference design separates retrieval evaluation from answer evaluation and carries freshness and revision fields in evidence. These signals allow a host to assess different failure modes rather than collapse quality into a single score.
questions.Risk: High retrieval recall does not establish answer correctness. A heuristic overlap score also cannot establish that a reasoning step is valid or that the source itself is authoritative.
questions.Trade: Multiple metrics complicate release decisions but expose regressions that one average hides. The right acceptance criteria depend on the product's questions and corpus.
questions.Try: Construct four answers that each fail a different dimension. Explain which measurement and which code boundary would reveal each failure.

questions.Q: What are the main cost and latency stages in a RAG request?
questions.A: Typical stages are query transformation, query embedding, candidate search, fusion, reranking, evidence assembly, and host generation. Ingestion has separate extraction, chunking, embedding, and storage costs. The relative expense depends on providers, data size, network placement, and configuration; this reference design does not establish universal timings.
questions.Why: Separating candidate_k from final_k permits a larger search pool without necessarily sending every hit to generation. Telemetry records stage events and durations, and the embedding executor bounds concurrency and provider call duration when configured.
questions.Risk: Increasing query variants, candidate counts, and retries together can multiply load. No single semaphore controls an entire fleet or gives an end-to-end request deadline.
questions.Trade: Higher candidate recall often costs more latency and money. Optimize against a quality target using measured stage distributions, not guessed millisecond service requests.
questions.Try: Create a latency budget spreadsheet with p50 and p95 per stage and an overall deadline. Mark every number as a hypothesis until you measure it.

questions.Q: What does domain-agnostic mean, and what does it not solve?
questions.A: Domain-agnostic means the core can work with different application schemas, sources, settings, and storage implementations through explicit interfaces. It does not mean every domain has identical chunking needs, permissions, legal retention rules, or quality thresholds. Those knowledge rules remain part of the host's product design.
questions.Why: The retrieval service receives settings, sessions, version storage, embedders, and retrieval strategies rather than importing a host's models. The same core can serve a knowledge corpus or a support corpus while their adapters and evaluation datasets differ.
questions.Risk: Generic abstractions can hide important domain constraints if the host never models them. A tenant filter is useful only when trusted identity selects the correct scope and every storage path respects it.
questions.Trade: Reusability reduces coupling but requires deliberate integration work. A specialized application may be quicker initially and harder to reuse safely later.
questions.Try: Compare an HR policy assistant and a public FAQ assistant. List five knowledge rules that differ even if they use identical the retrieval service components.

title: Architecture and design patterns
subtitle: Understand the dependency boundaries and why each seam exists.

questions.Q: Why separate a reusable retrieval subsystem from a complete application?
questions.A: The package supplies composable RAG infrastructure while the host owns application models, authentication, routing, deployment, and generation. That boundary allows an existing backend to adopt retrieval without letting a library control its domain schema or request lifecycle.
questions.Why: Expose retrieval, ingestion, and evidence contracts independently from web routes and business models. The host binds authentication, persistence, and generation policy. This makes components testable without implying that every backend is interchangeable.
questions.Risk: Integration errors move to the seams: missing scope policy, incorrect transaction ownership, or a fake embedder accidentally used for real search. Examples and contract tests help, but the host must review its wiring.
questions.Trade: You gain control and portability while doing more assembly. A packaged application would offer faster initial setup with more predetermined choices.
questions.Try: Draw a ports-and-adapters diagram showing which side owns users, SQL tables, provider credentials, evidence, and chat responses.

questions.Q: How does dependency inversion appear in the reference design?
questions.A: A fluent builder assembles collaborators through readable configuration methods and a final construction step. It can provide safe local defaults while requiring explicit production dependencies. The builder is a convenience facade; the lower-level contracts remain useful independently.
questions.Why: The ingestion coordinator accepts its collaborators in the constructor. the version repository receives the active session for mutations, and a SQL adapter interface abstracts database operations. You can replace a collaborator with a controlled test implementation without rewriting orchestration.
questions.Risk: An adapter can satisfy a Python method signature while violating atomicity or isolation semantics. Structural compatibility is weaker than behavioral compatibility, so tests need to exercise the promised guarantees.
questions.Trade: Interfaces add indirection and documentation work. They pay off when deployment stacks differ or when failure paths need deterministic testing.
questions.Try: Replace version storage with a tiny recording fake. Verify the order of find, close, create, delete, and upsert calls without assuming that call order alone proves rollback safety.

questions.Q: Why use Protocol instead of requiring every adapter to inherit a base class?
questions.A: Python Protocol supports structural typing: an object can satisfy a contract by providing the required members. This is useful when a host already has settings or session providers and should not need to inherit library-specific classes.
questions.Why: Retrieval settings and several storage seams express the attributes or methods consumers need. Some interfaces also use runtime_checkable, but runtime checks do not fully validate annotations, returned values, or transactional behavior.
questions.Risk: Duck typing can postpone integration errors until execution. Validate configuration at startup and run adapter contract tests; do not interpret isinstance against a protocol as a complete certification.
questions.Trade: Protocols reduce inheritance coupling while offering less shared implementation. Abstract base classes remain useful when construction rules or common behavior must be enforced.
questions.Try: Supply a dataclass as settings, then remove a required attribute. Compare static type feedback with the eventual runtime failure.

questions.Q: What does the Fluent Builder pattern contribute here?
questions.A: A retrieval-service builder assembles collaborators through readable configuration methods and an asynchronous build step. The local constructor chooses in-memory defaults while still requiring an embedding function. The result is a convenient facade over the lower-level components.
questions.Why: This keeps a small experiment short while allowing chunkers, stores, version stores, and settings to be replaced. The builder is composition convenience; it does not make an in-memory setup durable or create a learned local embedding model.
questions.Risk: Hidden defaults can be carried into production. Review the resolved store, embedding dimension, scope policy, and state retention before deploying an instance built for local use.
questions.Trade: A builder is easier to discover than a large constructor but adds another assembly surface to maintain. Direct constructors are clearer for unusual production wiring.
questions.Try: Run the offline quickstart, then rewrite its setup with explicit collaborators. Describe which defaults you would replace for a multi-worker service.

questions.Q: How are Factory, Registry, Strategy, and Adapter different patterns?
questions.A: A factory constructs a collaborator. A registry maps names to implementations. A strategy selects interchangeable behavior such as dense, lexical, or hybrid retrieval. An adapter translates an external API into the reference design's contract. The patterns solve different problems and often appear together.
questions.Why: Store factories and registries choose backend implementations; retrieval strategies compose search capabilities; backend classes translate vendor operations. This allows configuration-driven construction without forcing every search behavior into a storage class.
questions.Risk: A name-based registry can defer typos or missing optional dependency failures until runtime. Validate names and dependencies during startup, and avoid loading plugins based on arbitrary untrusted input.
questions.Trade: Configurable assembly improves extension but increases possible combinations. Support a documented matrix rather than assuming every registered backend supports every strategy and filter.
questions.Try: Explain how adding a new vector backend differs from adding a query reranker. Identify the construction, contract, and behavior changes separately.

questions.Q: Why split the vector-store interface into smaller capability protocols?
questions.A: A broad store interface is convenient when one backend supports every operation. Separate vector search, lexical search, fetch, and write capabilities let callers depend only on the operations they need. A keyword-only route should not require an embedding provider.
questions.Why: The retrieval service's retrieval strategies compose vector and lexical capabilities, permitting different backends for different signals. Capability declarations describe supported filters and guarantees before the strategy executes.
questions.Risk: A backend may advertise a capability it implements incompletely. Mandatory constraints should fail closed, and contract tests should verify semantics rather than only checking that methods exist.
questions.Trade: More interfaces create more concepts, but avoid fake implementations of unsupported methods. A single-store facade remains helpful for simple applications.
questions.Try: Design a lexical-only adapter. List the interfaces it needs and the vector-specific methods it should never have to emulate.

questions.Q: What does a SQL adapter interface abstract, and what remains PostgreSQL-specific?
questions.A: A SQL adapter interface abstracts session construction, execution, fetching, and advisory locking. It lets orchestration avoid direct dependence on one SQL library. It does not make PostgreSQL full-text functions or pgvector operators portable to an arbitrary database engine.
questions.Why: The PostgreSQL vector adapter still owns database-specific SQL. An alternative driver can implement the factory contract while preserving PostgreSQL semantics; a different database usually needs a different storage adapter and capability declaration.
questions.Risk: Replacing the driver without matching transaction and lock behavior can invalidate ingestion guarantees. A no-op advisory-lock implementation is not an equivalent production replacement.
questions.Trade: The extra seam improves driver flexibility and testability but carries semantic obligations. Direct driver calls would be simpler and more tightly coupled.
questions.Try: Write down the minimum behavior an async database driver adapter must preserve for a locked ingestion transaction. Include failure and rollback cases.

questions.Q: Why use dataclasses and explicit converters at API boundaries?
questions.A: Dataclasses make fields, defaults, and meanings discoverable without requiring a validation framework. Explicit converters keep dictionary-based adapters compatible while typed consumers work with Document, SearchResult, RetrievalRequest, and RetrievalResponse.
questions.Why: As_dicts and typed retrieval bridges separate legacy shapes from newer APIs. This supports gradual adoption without forcing every host and backend to migrate simultaneously.
questions.Risk: Type annotations alone do not validate hostile input, and conversions can lose fields such as reranker scores if an older result type does not represent them. Validate transport input and choose the typed response when you need its richer score information.
questions.Trade: Compatibility layers cost code and can preserve ambiguity. Removing them simplifies internals but may break downstream callers; a migration policy must be explicit.
questions.Try: Convert one typed hit to a dictionary and back. Check identity, metadata, distance, RRF score, and reranker score separately.

questions.Q: How does the Null Object pattern appear in telemetry?
questions.A: A a null event sink implements the event-sink contract while doing nothing. Consumers can emit an event without checking whether telemetry is configured at every call site. This keeps optional observability out of the main control flow.
questions.Why: Constructors select a null sink when no sink is supplied. A real sink can later export sanitized events, and the business path can retain the same call structure.
questions.Risk: A null sink can make missing production instrumentation invisible. Also inspect whether a supplied sink can raise or block; optional observability should not accidentally become an uncontrolled availability dependency.
questions.Trade: Fewer branches improve readability, while silent default behavior requires explicit operational verification. An application may choose mandatory instrumentation at its composition root.
questions.Try: Run the same retrieval with a recording sink and a null sink. Verify equal results and inspect which dimensions the recording sink receives.

questions.Q: How should I defend the architecture in an interview without inventing author intent?
questions.A: Describe observed boundaries, explain the problems they address, and distinguish inference from documented intent. For example, injected sessions support host transaction ownership; you can infer a portability benefit without claiming the author measured it against every ORM or framework.
questions.Why: Tie architectural explanations to an invariant and a failure scenario. For example, caller-owned transactions allow a business update and an outbox record to commit together. Explain the consequences without inventing historical author intent.
questions.Risk: Repeating comments as guarantees can mislead. Some comments simplify current behavior: the generic hybrid strategy awaits stages sequentially, and sliding-window chunks use UUIDs rather than universally deterministic IDs.
questions.Trade: Qualified service requests sound less absolute but survive technical scrutiny. A good design defense acknowledges obligations pushed to host adapters and conditions under which another design would win.
questions.Try: Prepare a five-minute defense with three source references, two explicit limitations, and one alternative architecture you would choose under different requirements.

title: Sources, connectors, and extraction
subtitle: Reliable knowledge starts with knowing what was actually scanned.

questions.Q: Why distinguish discovery, fetching, extraction, and ingestion?
questions.A: Discovery enumerates source items. Fetching obtains bytes. Extraction converts those bytes into usable text and provenance. Ingestion chunks, embeds, and indexes the result. Keeping these boundaries separate lets the same extraction or indexing logic serve several source systems.
questions.Why: Connector records carry discovery and load status, while a source-document record carries content and source metadata into the pipeline. A PDF extraction failure is therefore different from an empty bucket or an embedding provider outage.
questions.Risk: Flattening every failure into an empty list can cause a later reconciliation to delete healthy knowledge. The connector contract represents errors and whether a result is authoritative; the pipeline refuses non-authoritative a typed scan result mutation.
questions.Trade: Rich status handling takes more code than returning strings. It supports safe retries, deletion decisions, and actionable diagnostics.
questions.Try: Trace a PDF in an object bucket through all four stages. Specify the returned status when each stage fails and which stages can be retried independently.

questions.Q: What makes a source scan authoritative?
questions.A: An authoritative scan represents the complete intended snapshot under its configured scope and traversal rules. A successful first page is not a complete snapshot. Authority also depends on whether errors, limits, or missing pages could have hidden existing documents.
questions.Why: A typed scan result distinguishes completeness and status; sync uses that authority to infer removals. The ordinary ingestion pipeline skips a non-authoritative a typed scan result rather than replacing its current indexed content with a partial view.
questions.Risk: Treating a timeout or permission error as authoritative emptiness can erase knowledge. Conversely, never trusting a complete empty scan leaves deleted content searchable. Both require explicit semantics.
questions.Trade: Conservative authority rules may delay deletion after a source outage. That delay is preferable to interpreting an incomplete traversal as proof of absence, but access revocation needs a separate immediate control.
questions.Try: Simulate a three-page source where page two fails. Explain why the successfully fetched documents do not prove that all missing documents were deleted.

questions.Q: How should pagination and checkpoints work for incremental ingestion?
questions.A: A cursor identifies where enumeration should continue; a checkpoint records safely processed progress. They are not interchangeable. Saving a cursor before the corresponding data is activated can skip work after a crash, while saving too late can repeat work.
questions.Why: Connectors expose page and full-load methods, and sync checkpoints are guarded by the example fencing token. Idempotency and complete-snapshot reconciliation make repeated pages safer than silently losing them.
questions.Risk: Sources may mutate between pages, causing duplicates or omissions even if every request succeeds. Stable ordering, source-side snapshot tokens where available, deduplication, and periodic full reconciliation are integration concerns.
questions.Trade: Full scans simplify reconciliation but cost more source I/O. Incremental feeds are faster but require careful resume and deletion semantics.
questions.Try: Draw crashes immediately before activation, after activation, and after checkpoint saving. State which records will repeat and why no record should be skipped.

questions.Q: How does the directory connector reduce filesystem risks?
questions.A: Directory ingestion must constrain traversal to an intended root, apply inclusion knowledge rules, bound resource use, and avoid unsafe path or symlink behavior. The connector implements explicit open, target, and read helpers rather than blindly opening every discovered string.
questions.Why: The directory adapter also records intentional skips separately from scan errors. That distinction preserves the meaning of completeness: a deliberately excluded file is not the same as an inaccessible file that should have been included.
questions.Risk: A local filesystem is not automatically trusted. Permission changes and concurrent file replacement can occur during scanning, and host deployment permissions still determine what the process can access.
questions.Trade: Strict traversal and file knowledge rules can exclude legitimate sources and need configuration. Broad scanning is easier to start and harder to secure or make reproducible.
questions.Try: Read the directory connector's _open and _target helpers. Build a small temporary corpus containing ignored files, nested directories, and a symlink, and predict the reported skips.

questions.Q: Why does an HTTP connector need SSRF protection?
questions.A: Server-Side Request Forgery occurs when a server fetches a destination chosen through untrusted input and reaches internal services or metadata endpoints. A document URL can be an attack input just as an API parameter can.
questions.Why: The HTTP connector validates destinations, pins requests to an approved public IP, disables automatic redirects, and checks redirects explicitly. It rejects attempts to turn off its network protections. Website crawling requires explicit allowed domains.
questions.Risk: Domain checking alone cannot stop DNS rebinding or redirect-based bypasses. Egress policy, deployment DNS behavior, and the actual client transport also matter. Treat source fetching as a separate trust boundary.
questions.Trade: Public-only fetching limits access to legitimate private knowledge services. Supporting private services safely requires a deliberately trusted integration rather than a blanket bypass of URL validation.
questions.Try: Inspect the checks before and after a redirect. Explain why allowing example.com does not authorize a redirect to a loopback address.

questions.Q: How should HTTP rate limits, redirects, and partial crawls affect indexing?
questions.A: Rate limits and timeouts indicate unavailable or incomplete source access, not document deletion. Redirects may change origin and therefore change what credentials may safely be forwarded. Crawl limits bound work but can also prevent a complete snapshot.
questions.Why: The connector tracks statuses such as rate-limited or incomplete traversal, checks redirect destinations, and rejects authenticated cross-origin redirects. Sync can use result authority to decide whether removal inference is permissible.
questions.Risk: Retrying an incomplete scan without bounds can overload the source; accepting it as complete can remove data. A bounded source request still needs a host scheduling and retry policy for repeated jobs.
questions.Trade: Tight crawl limits improve predictability while reducing corpus coverage. Completeness must reflect the limit rather than presenting the bounded subset as the whole source.
questions.Try: Design a crawl that reaches its configured limit exactly. Determine from the connector's terminal state whether it is authoritative, rather than guessing from the number of returned pages.

questions.Q: What identity and consistency issues arise with object storage?
questions.A: Object keys identify source items, but content can change under the same key. ETags, version identifiers, metadata, and content hashes can describe different aspects of revision identity. An ETag should not automatically be treated as a universal content checksum.
questions.Why: An object-storage adapter separates listing and reading and returns provenance through a source-document record. Its full-load path must account for continuation tokens and errors before a scan can authorize removal of absent objects.
questions.Risk: Listing and fetching can observe different moments. A host needing exact historical verification should retain source versions or snapshots rather than assuming the latest object body matches a previous citation.
questions.Trade: Versioned reads and snapshot retention cost storage and integration work. Reading only current objects is simpler but weakens reproducibility.
questions.Try: Change one object between listing and download. Describe which metadata lets you detect or explain the observed revision and which guarantees the source must provide.

questions.Q: Why is text extraction part of the retrieval quality problem?
questions.A: Search cannot recover information that extraction discarded or scrambled. PDF reading order, tables, headings, repeated headers, and image-only pages can distort the indexed text. Extraction quality therefore sets an upper bound on downstream retrieval quality.
questions.Why: Extractors are separate adapters and extractor identity participates in ingestion fingerprints. Changing extraction behavior can require reindexing even if the underlying file bytes did not change.
questions.Risk: A successful parse may still yield semantically broken text. The reference design does not supply a universal OCR or table-understanding guarantee; inspect output and use host-selected extractors where needed.
questions.Trade: Rich document parsing improves structure at the cost of dependencies, compute, and more failure modes. Plain text extraction is easier to operate but can lose relationships that answers depend on.
questions.Try: Extract a two-column page and a table. Compare the text to the source visually, then write a retrieval question that fails if cell relationships are lost.

questions.Q: Which source metadata must survive into evidence?
questions.A: Preserve stable source and document identity, revision, title or section, location or offsets where available, and the relevant isolation scope. These fields support deletion, attribution, source opening, and debugging. They are not decorative labels added after search.
questions.Why: The ingestion coordinator merges document and chunk metadata and stamps the actual source name. It also forwards external_id, provenance, location, and extractor information. Evidence types then normalize attribution fields for consumers.
questions.Risk: Metadata may contain secrets or untrusted URLs. Sanitizing a displayed URI is not the same as safely fetching it, and arbitrary metadata should not automatically be logged or rendered as HTML.
questions.Trade: Rich metadata adds storage and schema complexity. Omitting it makes early indexing easy but later provenance reconstruction unreliable.
questions.Try: Trace the metadata of two documents with different sources through one ingestion run. Verify that every chunk retains the correct source instead of inheriting one global source label.

questions.Q: Why are watchers insufficient without reconciliation?
questions.A: A watcher provides low-latency change notifications, but notifications can be missed during downtime, buffer overflow, or process failure. A periodic reconciliation compares the source's current authoritative state against indexed state and repairs divergence.
questions.Why: The directory module includes watcher and periodic reconciler helpers. Sync plans classify additions, changes, removals, metadata-only updates, and unchanged items so a full comparison need not re-embed everything.
questions.Risk: Assuming an event stream is complete leaves permanently stale knowledge after a missed event. Deletion events also need an explicit target; absence of an event is not proof that an item still exists.
questions.Trade: Combining watchers with scans spends extra source I/O but improves eventual correctness. Full scans alone are simpler when freshness requirements are modest.
questions.Try: Stop the watcher, edit and delete files, then resume it. Describe how a scheduled reconciliation repairs changes that the live event stream never delivered.

title: Chunking and document structure
subtitle: Treat chunking as an information boundary, not a magic constant.

questions.Q: Why chunk documents at all?
questions.A: Chunking creates retrieval units small enough to match a question and fit a context budget. A whole manual can contain many unrelated topics; embedding it as one vector blends signals and returning all of it wastes context. A tiny fragment can lose the conditions that make its meaning correct.
questions.Why: The retrieval service injects a Chunker into ingestion. This makes chunking a replaceable strategy whose version and configuration participate in snapshot comparison, rather than an untracked preprocessing script.
questions.Risk: A boundary can separate a rule from its exception or a table heading from its values. Overlap and section-aware parsing mitigate some boundary loss, but only corpus-specific evaluation reveals whether the chosen units preserve meaning.
questions.Trade: Smaller chunks improve targeting and increase index size; larger chunks preserve context and can dilute relevance. There is no universally best chunk size.
questions.Try: Split the same policy into small and large chunks. Use questions about exceptions and compare whether each retrieved unit contains enough information to answer safely.

questions.Q: Does a sliding-window chunker count tokens, words, or characters?
questions.A: It counts whitespace-separated words using text.split(). chunk_size and overlap therefore measure words. They do not define a model tokenizer's context size, and they do not behave identically for every language or code-heavy input.
questions.Why: The implementation steps through words by chunk_size minus overlap and rejoins each slice. This simple algorithm has no model dependency and is suitable as a transparent baseline.
questions.Risk: Treating 600 words as 600 tokens can overflow a downstream budget. Languages without whitespace and punctuation-heavy text can also produce surprising retrieval units. The evidence layer has a separate tokenizer abstraction for context accounting.
questions.Trade: Word splitting is fast and dependency-free, while token-aware or structure-aware splitting can better match actual model and document constraints.
questions.Try: Chunk an English paragraph, a Python file, and Arabic text with identical settings. Count actual model tokens separately and compare the ratios.

questions.Q: How does overlap affect recall and ingestion cost?
questions.A: Overlap repeats material near neighboring boundaries so that a question spanning a split still has a chance to retrieve a coherent chunk. The stride is chunk_size minus overlap. With long text, the repetition factor is roughly chunk_size divided by stride, ignoring the final partial window.
questions.Why: For size 600 and overlap 100, the stride is 500 and the approximate repeated-word factor is 1.2. This is a mathematical estimate of chunked input, not a measured provider billing factor or a quality guarantee.
questions.Risk: Excessive overlap produces near-duplicate hits and increases embedding work. Evidence deduplication and eligible span merging reduce redundant context, but they do not undo ingestion cost.
questions.Trade: More overlap can improve boundary coverage while reducing diversity among top hits. Tune against a labeled question set rather than maximizing repetition.
questions.Try: Calculate chunk counts for 1,100 words at several overlaps, then verify them with sliding_window_chunk. Explain why the loop stops after the final covered window.

questions.Q: Why validate that overlap is smaller than chunk_size?
questions.A: The stride must be positive for the window to advance. An overlap equal to the chunk size creates a zero stride; a larger overlap creates an invalid or backward progression. These are algorithm validity constraints, not optional quality preferences.
questions.Why: Both the function and the chunker constructor validate positive size and overlap in the interval from zero inclusive to size exclusive. Invalid configuration fails early before ingestion mutates versions or spends embedding calls.
questions.Risk: A malformed chunking configuration can block all ingestion or unexpectedly produce no chunks. Startup validation and focused boundary tests make such failures easier to diagnose than late failures inside a scheduled job.
questions.Trade: Strict validation rejects configurations that a permissive implementation might silently repair. Silent repair would conceal the actual indexing configuration and make snapshot identity less meaningful.
questions.Try: Exercise zero size, negative overlap, overlap equal to size, and empty text. Distinguish invalid configuration from a valid empty result.

questions.Q: How does a section-aware chunker preserve semantic structure?
questions.A: It splits Markdown on H2 headings, reconstructs a section with its title, and delegates that section to an inner chunker. Section titles therefore participate in embedded text rather than existing only as metadata. The inner strategy still controls subdivision of a long section.
questions.Why: Composition reuses the sliding-window algorithm while adding section, chunk index, and sub-chunk index metadata. File reading remains in the source adapter; the chunker operates on text.
questions.Risk: A regular expression for H2 headings is not a complete Markdown parser. Unusual markup and headings inside fenced code can create misleading boundaries. Evaluate actual corpus syntax before relying on section semantics.
questions.Trade: This wrapper is lightweight and understandable, while a full syntax-tree parser handles richer structure at higher implementation and dependency cost.
questions.Try: Use a document with a preamble, H2 sections, H3 headings, and a fenced code sample containing a heading-like line. Inspect the exact emitted chunk text.

questions.Q: Are chunk IDs deterministic in this implementation?
questions.A: Chunk IDs may be content-derived, position-derived, randomly generated, or scoped to an index generation. No choice is universally stable. Define identity around the operations it must support: deduplication, revision tracking, source lookup, and safe replacement.
questions.Why: Store document revision, span, chunker profile, and generation separately where needed. Test repeated chunking and document edits; stable identity requires an explicit contract rather than an assumption about UUIDs.
questions.Risk: Conflating position metadata with the actual store ID can break deduplication, deletion, and citation mapping. Comments about position-based chunk identifiers should be interpreted in the relevant adapter context, not generalized to every chunker.
questions.Trade: Random physical IDs avoid some collisions but need lifecycle tracking. Deterministic IDs simplify repeat writes but must include enough scope and revision information to avoid accidental replacement.
questions.Try: Chunk identical input twice, edit a paragraph, and compare the identity guarantees of content-based, positional, and generation-scoped IDs.

questions.Q: Why must chunker configuration be part of an ingestion fingerprint?
questions.A: The same source text produces a different index when chunk size, overlap, section handling, or algorithm version changes. Hashing only file content would incorrectly classify that index as current and skip the required rebuild.
questions.Why: The snapshot builder records chunker identity, version, and sanitized configuration alongside source and embedding information. snapshot_matches therefore represents compatibility of the indexing process rather than only equality of input bytes.
questions.Risk: A custom chunker that hides meaningful configuration can keep stale vectors active after a behavior change. A version property is useful only if maintainers update it when output semantics change.
questions.Trade: Detailed fingerprints trigger more rebuilds and improve reproducibility. Minimal fingerprints save work while making silent configuration drift more likely.
questions.Try: Ingest unchanged text, change overlap, and ingest again. Verify that the snapshot changes even though the source hash remains equal.

questions.Q: What would parent-child or hierarchical retrieval add?
questions.A: Parent-child retrieval searches fine-grained child chunks, then expands selected hits into a larger parent section or document for context. Hierarchical retrieval can first choose a topic or summary and then search within it. These are design extensions, not a default pipeline implemented by this reference design.
questions.Why: The retrieval service's metadata, fetch capabilities, and evidence assembly seams provide useful building blocks, but a host must implement expansion, identity mapping, authorization, and evaluation. Expansion should occur before final budgeting so its actual rendered size is counted.
questions.Risk: Parent expansion can expose unauthorized neighboring text or overwhelm context. A child being authorized does not automatically authorize every parent span or sibling chunk.
questions.Trade: More context may resolve ambiguity while increasing latency and irrelevant material. A simple section-aware chunker may be sufficient for a small structured corpus.
questions.Try: Design an extension that expands a hit to its section. State which metadata is required and where scope checks and budget checks must run.

questions.Q: How should chunking change for code, tables, and multilingual documents?
questions.A: Use boundaries that preserve the relationships questions depend on: functions and classes for code, row and column context for tables, and language-appropriate segmentation for text. A word window is a baseline, not proof that all these formats retain their semantics.
questions.Why: The Chunker protocol lets a host substitute a parser-based strategy without changing the entire ingestion pipeline. Metadata can preserve symbols, table identifiers, or locations for evidence presentation.
questions.Risk: Combining unrelated rows or truncating a function's preconditions can generate a misleading answer from faithfully quoted text. Arbitrary structure metadata also needs stable versioning and source lookup support.
questions.Trade: Specialized chunkers improve some domains while increasing maintenance and creating less comparable retrieval units. Maintain a shared evaluation interface across them.
questions.Try: Build three questions that require a function's error branch, a table's unit header, and a multilingual synonym. Compare a structural chunker with the word-window baseline.

questions.Q: How do I tune chunking scientifically?
questions.A: Hold the corpus, query set, embedding profile, backend settings, and evaluation procedure fixed while varying chunking. Measure retrieval recall and rank, evidence fit, answer faithfulness, index size, and embedding volume. Record configurations so the result is reproducible.
questions.Why: The retrieval service separates chunking from embedding and evaluation, making controlled experiments possible. Its snapshots help identify configuration changes, but they are not an experiment tracker by themselves.
questions.Risk: Optimizing on a handful of visible questions overfits the benchmark. Split tuning and held-out questions and include boundary cases, exact identifiers, long sections, and unanswerable queries.
questions.Trade: A full grid search costs indexing time. Start with a small set of plausible configurations and investigate failure examples before expanding the search.
questions.Try: Compare three sizes with two overlaps and publish a table containing quality, indexed chunk count, and estimated embedding input. Explain the winning configuration's remaining failure cases.

title: Embeddings and resilient execution
subtitle: Protect vector compatibility, provider capacity, and tenant data.

questions.Q: What is an embedding, and why is its dimension not enough to identify it?
questions.A: An embedding maps input text to a vector whose geometry supports a similarity task. Dimension is the number of coordinates, not an identity for the learned space. Two providers can both return 1,536 numbers while placing meanings in incompatible coordinate systems.
questions.Why: An embedding profile records provider, endpoint, model, revision, dimension, normalization, metric, task mode, and preprocessing configuration. Its canonical hash gives the indexing configuration a stable identity that can be carried into snapshots and caches.
questions.Risk: Mixing incompatible document and query vectors can produce plausible but meaningless nearest neighbors without a shape error. Dimension validation catches only one class of incompatibility.
questions.Trade: Rich profile identity makes model migrations safer but requires reindexing discipline and additional metadata. Reusing an index based only on equal dimension is cheaper and unreliable.
questions.Try: Define two profiles with the same dimension and different models. Explain why a successful database insert would not prove they can share one search space.

questions.Q: Why distinguish document and query embedding modes?
questions.A: Some embedding models are trained asymmetrically: a short question and a longer passage use different task instructions or modes but remain in a compatible retrieval space. Symmetric models use the same treatment for both. The correct mode is part of the model's intended retrieval contract.
questions.Why: A task mode represents DOCUMENT, QUERY, and SYMMETRIC. Query-vector helpers can call embed_query, while document processing can use document embedding methods. Profile compatibility deliberately allows different task modes for an otherwise matching pair.
questions.Risk: A generic callable may erase mode distinctions unless the adapter implements them correctly. Also, the compatibility helper does not compare preprocessing_config, so custom instruction compatibility needs additional validation.
questions.Trade: Task-aware interfaces improve provider fidelity but add API surface. A plain callable remains convenient for simple symmetric embedders and offline demonstrations.
questions.Try: Inspect a custom adapter's query and document paths. Verify the instructions each sends and explain whether profile equality or query compatibility is the appropriate check.

questions.Q: How do cosine, dot product, and L2 differ?
questions.A: Cosine compares direction, dot product combines alignment and magnitude, and L2 measures Euclidean separation. For unit-normalized vectors, squared L2 equals two minus twice the dot product, and dot product equals cosine similarity. Without normalization, those ranking relationships need not hold.
questions.Why: Profile enums describe metric and normalization. Stores translate the chosen metric into their backend semantics, while result scores distinguish lower-is-better distance from higher-is-better relevance.
questions.Risk: A threshold calibrated for one metric cannot safely be reused for another. Unknown dimensions and unnormalized vectors can also make low-level helpers behave unexpectedly if callers bypass validation.
questions.Trade: Cosine often fits directional semantic comparisons; dot product may intentionally use norm information. The right choice follows the embedding model and index configuration, then empirical evaluation.
questions.Try: Compare vectors [1,0], [2,0], and [0,1] under all three measures. Predict which pairs tie and why normalization changes the answer.

questions.Q: What validation should happen before storing embedding responses?
questions.A: Check one vector per input, the expected dimension, and finite numeric values. Preserve input-output order. A response with fewer vectors must fail rather than silently pair only a prefix of the chunks with embeddings.
questions.Why: A bounded embedding executor validates response count and geometry; the ingestion coordinator uses strict zip alignment and validates each chunk vector before mutation. Preparation failures therefore occur before the version-switching critical section.
questions.Risk: Valid shape does not prove semantic quality or correct provider task mode. A constant vector can pass shape validation and still destroy retrieval usefulness, so quality evaluation remains separate.
questions.Trade: Validation costs a pass over returned coordinates but prevents durable index corruption that is expensive to diagnose later. Skipping it is only a superficial throughput optimization.
questions.Try: Use fake providers returning too few vectors, wrong dimensions, NaN, and identical finite vectors. Identify which failures validation catches and which require a retrieval test.

questions.Q: How do retries and exponential backoff help without fixing every outage?
questions.A: Retries can recover transient network, rate-limit, and service failures. Exponential backoff delays repeated attempts; jitter reduces synchronized retry bursts. Permanent authentication, configuration, and dimension errors should fail promptly because identical retries are unlikely to help.
questions.Why: A bounded embedding executor classifies exceptions, honors exposed Retry-After hints, applies a retry ceiling, and validates responses. Cancellation is propagated rather than treated as another retryable failure.
questions.Risk: Classification includes message-pattern heuristics and treats unknown errors as transient. Misclassification can waste calls, and Retry-After can extend operation duration. The host still needs an overall deadline and provider-specific error handling where necessary.
questions.Trade: More retries improve recovery probability while increasing tail latency, cost, and load during an outage. Bound them against the request's purpose and budget.
questions.Try: Simulate two transient failures followed by success, then a permanent failure. Record attempts and delays using injected clock and sleep functions.

questions.Q: What do concurrency limits, queue bounds, and backpressure actually mean here?
questions.A: A semaphore limits simultaneous work inside one execution scope. A bounded queue limits waiting items. Backpressure controls how producers react when capacity is exhausted. None alone establishes a fleet-wide capacity limit.
questions.Why: Combine a bounded producer queue, explicit worker concurrency, request deadlines, and shared provider quotas where needed. Instrument queue time separately from provider latency; an async batch is not a durable job.
questions.Risk: Many waiting tasks or many process-local executors can still overwhelm memory or a shared provider quota. The host needs admission control and, when appropriate, a bounded job queue and shared quota policy.
questions.Trade: Small concurrency limits protect providers and increase waiting latency. Larger values improve throughput until the actual service or connection pool saturates.
questions.Try: Launch many calls through one executor and then through several instances. Measure in-flight operations and explain why a process-local semaphore is not a global rate limiter.

questions.Q: How does embedding caching preserve isolation and compatibility?
questions.A: Cache identity combines isolation scope, content hash, embedding profile hash, and task mode. Reusing a vector is safe only when these semantic inputs match the deployment's policy. A content hash alone is insufficient for model changes or tenant isolation.
questions.Why: A scoped embedding cache uses scoped keys by default, copies vectors on storage and retrieval, supports LRU capacity and optional TTL, and requires explicit opt-in for cross-tenant sharing. It is an in-process component, not a distributed cache.
questions.Risk: Cross-tenant reuse can leak equality signals or complicate retention obligations. The class is not thread-safe, and TTL expiry alone is not immediate revocation. The host must align cache scope and purge behavior with its privacy policy.
questions.Trade: More isolation reduces hit rate while keeping independent data lifecycles manageable. Shared caching saves calls but needs a justified policy.
questions.Try: Cache identical content in two scopes with different profiles and task modes. Verify the allowed hits and test scope invalidation.

questions.Q: How should an embedding model migration be rolled out?
questions.A: Treat a vector-space change as a new index generation. Build and validate new vectors without mixing them into the old query space, evaluate quality, activate the new generation, and retain a rollback plan. Query embeddings must switch compatibly with the active documents.
questions.Why: Profiles_require_reindex compares canonical hashes, while ingestion snapshots and sync generation mechanisms support detecting configuration changes and controlling visibility. They provide building blocks, not a complete deployment orchestrator for every backend.
questions.Risk: Switching only the query model can silently degrade retrieval. Reusing caches or thresholds calibrated for the old profile can also invalidate conclusions even if dimensions remain equal.
questions.Trade: Parallel generations need extra storage and embedding cost but permit verification before cutover. In-place replacement is cheaper and harder to roll back safely.
questions.Try: Write a migration checklist with a shadow evaluation, profile hash check, activation condition, and rollback trigger. State how queries choose the active profile.

questions.Q: Why can a hashing embedder demonstrate plumbing but not semantic intelligence?
questions.A: The quickstart hashes tokens into a small vector and normalizes it. Shared words produce shared coordinates, making an offline demonstration deterministic and cheap. It has no learned semantic representation and cannot reliably associate paraphrases that share little vocabulary.
questions.Why: A retrieval-service builder.local requires an injected embedder; core does not ship pretrained neural weights. The example deliberately supplies a fake so build, ingest, and search can run without API keys or external services.
questions.Risk: Treating success on that example as proof of production retrieval quality confuses system integration with representation learning. Hash collisions can also make unrelated text appear close in a tiny space.
questions.Trade: A fake is excellent for controlled tests and onboarding, while a learned provider is needed to evaluate realistic semantic behavior. Keep those purposes distinct.
questions.Try: Search with a synonym-only paraphrase and compare it to an exact-word query. Explain the difference using the hashing algorithm rather than attributing it to an LLM.

questions.Q: How should I measure embedding throughput and cost responsibly?
questions.A: Track documents and tokens processed, batches, retries, cache hits, provider latency, and validation failures. Estimate total spend using actual provider usage where available; heuristic token estimates are useful for scheduling but are not billing records.
questions.Why: Embedding metrics and telemetry support operational accounting, while the executor splits batches and can enforce a soft estimated-input cap. Separating preparation from transactions prevents slow provider calls from unnecessarily occupying ingestion locks.
questions.Risk: Average latency hides retries and tail behavior. A low per-batch cost can become expensive when overlap, query expansion, and repeated full indexing multiply input volume.
questions.Trade: Detailed metrics improve tuning while high-cardinality labels and raw text logging create overhead and privacy risks. Prefer aggregated, sanitized dimensions.
questions.Try: Compare a cold ingestion with an unchanged-source rerun and a model-change rerun. Attribute work saved by snapshot skipping separately from cache hits.

title: Vector storage and database design
subtitle: Choose guarantees as carefully as similarity algorithms.

questions.Q: What does a vector database store besides vectors?
questions.A: A useful retrieval record contains identity, text or a text reference, a vector, and filterable metadata. Production systems also need revision and scope information, deletion semantics, and an explicit persistence model. A fast nearest-neighbor API alone does not provide those guarantees.
questions.Why: The retrieval service's store contracts combine or separate writing, vector search, lexical search, fetch, and deletion. Backend capability declarations describe which operations and constraints the adapter actually supports.
questions.Risk: An index that returns similar vectors but cannot enforce a required tenant filter is unsuitable for that request. Capability validation rejects unsupported mandatory constraints instead of silently ignoring them.
questions.Trade: A general-purpose database can unify transactional metadata and vectors; a specialist engine can offer different scaling and operational features. Compare the adapter's concrete guarantees rather than category labels.
questions.Try: Create a decision matrix for persistence, filters, lexical search, transactions, generation visibility, and deletion latency for two candidate backends.

questions.Q: Why use PostgreSQL with pgvector and full-text search?
questions.A: PostgreSQL can combine relational filters, vector distance, lexical ranking, and host-managed transactions in one database. This is attractive when the application already depends on PostgreSQL and wants retrieval to participate in existing data governance.
questions.Why: The PostgreSQL vector adapter builds table-agnostic SQL from validated identifiers and uses database-specific search operations. The host supplies schema and sessions; the adapter does not turn every database into PostgreSQL or own every application migration.
questions.Risk: Database extension setup, indexes, pool sizing, and query plans still need operational care. The presence of pgvector does not prove that an approximate index is configured or used for a particular query.
questions.Trade: One database reduces cross-system coordination but couples workloads and capacity. A separate vector service isolates scaling while introducing another consistency and authorization boundary.
questions.Try: Explain what an EXPLAIN plan would need to show before you claim a vector query uses an ANN index. Keep that distinct from the Python adapter's API.

questions.Q: What is ANN, and how is it different from exact nearest-neighbor search?
questions.A: Approximate Nearest Neighbor search trades guaranteed exact ranking for faster search over large vector collections. Exact search compares against all eligible vectors and provides a useful correctness baseline. Algorithms such as HNSW and IVF have different memory, tuning, and recall behavior.
questions.Why: The retrieval service delegates vector operations to backends. An in-memory scan is useful for small controlled examples; a production backend may use an approximate index depending on its configuration and query plan. ANN is not universally forced by this library.
questions.Risk: ANN can miss relevant candidates before reranking ever sees them. Metadata filters and small candidate pools can interact with index behavior, so recall must be measured under actual constraints.
questions.Trade: Higher search effort usually improves recall and costs latency or memory. Exact search may be sufficient for small corpora or useful as an offline oracle.
questions.Try: Compare approximate results with exact results on the same authorized subset. Plot recall versus latency while varying backend search effort.

questions.Q: Why are native lexical search and token-overlap fallback not equivalent?
questions.A: PostgreSQL full-text search provides language configuration, query parsing, and ranking facilities. The shared fallback tokenizes lowercase ASCII alphanumeric sequences and scores query-token overlap. It is a lightweight approximation, not BM25 and not equivalent multilingual search.
questions.Why: The scoring helper makes non-PostgreSQL backends usable in hybrid examples while capability declarations distinguish native and approximate lexical support. This preserves a common result shape without pretending the underlying ranking models are identical.
questions.Risk: Non-ASCII text and linguistic variation may behave poorly in the fallback. An evaluation that covers only English exact-word examples can miss this limitation.
questions.Trade: A portable fallback avoids another search service, while native full-text infrastructure generally offers richer lexical behavior. Choose according to corpus language and quality requirements.
questions.Try: Tokenize an Arabic query and an English product code using the fallback. Inspect the actual tokens before interpreting any hybrid score.

questions.Q: How does the reference design prevent SQL injection in dynamic queries?
questions.A: SQL values use bound parameters, while table and column names require separate identifier validation because SQL drivers cannot bind identifiers as ordinary values. the retrieval service validates dynamic names before interpolation into backend SQL.
questions.Why: The validation helper restricts identifiers to a simple allowlisted syntax. the PostgreSQL vector adapter applies validation when constructing operations and keeps values in parameter dictionaries. This is safer than escaping arbitrary user-provided SQL fragments.
questions.Risk: A valid identifier is not proof of authorization to access that table. Hosts must select trusted schema configuration and limit database permissions. Application transport validation also remains necessary.
questions.Trade: Strict names exclude qualified or unusual identifiers unless explicitly supported. That constraint simplifies safe SQL construction at the cost of some schema flexibility.
questions.Try: Compare a malicious value, a malicious table name, and a syntactically valid but unauthorized table name. Explain which layer must stop each one.

questions.Q: What does session injection buy, and when does atomicity fail?
questions.A: Session injection lets several operations join a transaction owned by the host or pipeline. When version mutations and vector writes truly use the same transactional database session, rollback can preserve the previous active state if a write fails.
questions.Why: The ingestion coordinator forwards the critical session into version storage and store upsert. Its guarantee depends on both adapters honoring that session. A remote vector service or in-memory store may not participate in the SQL transaction.
questions.Risk: Passing a session argument that an adapter ignores does not create cross-system atomicity. The sync path instead uses prepared generations and manifest visibility, with durable adapter obligations.
questions.Trade: Shared transactions simplify consistency within one database. Cross-service storage can scale independently but needs explicit visibility, retries, reconciliation, and failure recovery.
questions.Try: Draw a rollback scenario for PostgreSQL-only storage and another for SQL versions plus a remote vector engine. Identify the write that cannot be rolled back in the second design.

questions.Q: How do Qdrant, Chroma, FAISS, and in-memory adapters differ operationally?
questions.A: They expose a common retrieval surface but use different storage and execution models. In-memory state is process-local. FAISS is an indexing library whose surrounding metadata and persistence need attention. Service-backed engines introduce network and server configuration. Adapter support, not brand identity, determines available guarantees.
questions.Why: Each backend has its own implementation and optional dependency. The factory and capability layer let callers choose a backend while rejecting unsupported constraints instead of claiming complete interchangeability.
questions.Risk: Assuming identical durability, filter semantics, or transaction participation across these adapters can violate correctness. Inspect persistence and metadata behavior in the selected implementation and deployment.
questions.Trade: Lightweight local execution reduces setup; service-backed deployment supports different scale and operations needs. Portability often means accepting a common subset or explicitly branching on capabilities.
questions.Try: Compare three public backend configurations. Record where vectors and metadata live, which constraints they enforce, and what survives a process restart.

questions.Q: Why are strict error semantics important for storage operations?
questions.A: A failed query and a successful query with zero matches mean different things. Lenient APIs may log an error and return an empty list or zero count; that is convenient for some callers but dangerous when the host interprets emptiness as authoritative.
questions.Why: Retrieval supports strict mode and a typed retrieval error type. Mandatory capability and scope failures are designed to propagate rather than become silent fallbacks. Evidence assembly can represent backend failure distinctly when the host preserves that information.
questions.Risk: Forgetting strict mode can make an outage look like missing knowledge or an empty index. Health and deletion decisions should not infer success solely from an empty return value.
questions.Trade: Strict propagation requires explicit application error handling. Lenient fallback improves continuity only when the product can tolerate ambiguity and communicates it honestly.
questions.Try: Make the backend raise on search and count. Compare strict and lenient behavior and design the corresponding UI states.

questions.Q: How should deletion differ from physical garbage collection?
questions.A: Logical deletion removes permission or visibility immediately; physical cleanup later reservice requests index storage. Separating the two prevents asynchronous vector deletion from remaining an access-control dependency.
questions.Why: Sync manifests can tombstone documents, and a synchronous retrieval adapter validates status, generation, scope, and chunk membership before returning hits. Garbage collection removes retired or uncommitted vectors after visibility decisions.
questions.Risk: Calling the raw vector store bypasses manifest checks. A delayed physical deletion is safe only if every reader uses the required visibility boundary and source lookup also respects revocation.
questions.Trade: Manifest gating adds reads and coordination but permits conservative cleanup and safer recovery. Immediate physical deletion alone is simpler but can fail or lag.
questions.Try: Leave a tombstoned document's vectors physically present. Verify that the supported sync retrieval path returns no evidence and explain why raw nearest-neighbor access must remain internal.

questions.Q: What does a trustworthy backend capability contract look like?
questions.A: It states supported filter operators and features such as document fetch, deletion, scope enforcement, generation visibility, and transaction guarantees. Unsupported mandatory requirements produce an error before returning potentially unsafe results.
questions.Why: Store capability declarations validates both requested constraints and filter shapes. This makes backend selection a correctness decision rather than a best-effort call to methods that may silently ignore arguments.
questions.Risk: Declarations are assertions by adapter code. A falsely advertised capability is still a bug, and permissive host defaults can avoid requesting a guarantee that the product actually needs.
questions.Trade: Fail-closed behavior reduces surprising leakage but can reject configurations that previously appeared to work. That incompatibility is useful when the earlier behavior was unsafe or incomplete.
questions.Try: Build an adapter that rejects range filters and transactions. Send requests requiring each feature and verify rejection occurs before any evidence is returned.

title: Retrieval, fusion, and reranking
subtitle: Find candidates, enforce constraints, then spend ranking effort wisely.

questions.Q: What happens inside a typed retrieval request?
questions.A: RetrievalRequest carries the query, candidate and final counts, threshold, filters, isolation scope, expected generation, metadata projection, session, and mandatory capabilities. It makes execution constraints explicit instead of hiding them in loosely interpreted keyword arguments.
questions.Why: A hybrid retriever coerces legacy calls into this form and validates supported constraints before delegating to a store or strategy. Effective filters and required metadata help preserve scope checks across the execution path.
questions.Risk: A well-typed request can still contain an unauthorized scope if the host trusts the user's input. Authentication must establish which scope the caller is allowed to request.
questions.Trade: A richer request object improves composability and inspection but requires a stable public contract and deliberate defaults. A small positional API is easier for toy usage.
questions.Try: Construct one request for tenant A with a larger candidate pool and a smaller final result set. Explain every field that affects authorization, ranking, or visibility.

questions.Q: Why separate candidate_k from final_k?
questions.A: Candidate_k determines how many initial hits later stages can inspect; final_k determines how many results the caller receives. A reranker cannot promote a relevant passage that the candidate stage never retrieved. Fetching only five candidates and returning five wastes much of the value of reranking.
questions.Why: The strategy API carries both counts through retrieval and applies final slicing after optional reranking and scope validation. Evidence budgeting is yet another limit and should not be confused with either count.
questions.Risk: Very large candidate pools increase backend work, reranker cost, and exposure of material to external services. Candidates sent to a reranker must already respect applicable permissions.
questions.Trade: More candidates can improve recall with diminishing returns. Tune using recall, final ranking quality, and latency rather than assuming larger is always better.
questions.Try: Compare candidate pools of 10, 30, and 100 while holding final_k at five. Track whether missing answers were absent from the pool or simply ranked too low.

questions.Q: How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion work here?
questions.A: RRF sums reciprocal rank contributions from independent result lists. This implementation uses 1/(60 + rank) with one-based ranks, then sorts by descending sum and breaks ties by document ID. It avoids directly adding incomparable raw distance and keyword scores.
questions.Why: The shared rrf_merge helper constructs rank maps for vector and lexical lists. A document appearing in both gets two contributions; a document missing from a stage receives no contribution from that stage.
questions.Risk: RRF discards score magnitudes, so a near-tie and a decisive first-place win contribute identically at the same rank. Candidate truncation also limits which documents can benefit from fusion.
questions.Trade: Rank fusion is simple and robust across scoring scales, while weighted or learned fusion may capture more signal at the cost of calibration and training data.
questions.Try: Calculate scores for a document ranked first in one stage and another ranked tenth in both. Verify the ordering with rrf_merge and inspect deterministic ties.

questions.Q: Are dense and lexical stages executed concurrently?
questions.A: Dense and lexical search can run concurrently when they are independent and the backend supports the combined load. They can also run sequentially or inside one SQL statement. Choose deliberately and measure the actual execution path.
questions.Why: Parallelize independent I/O with a bounded task group and preserve separate failure outcomes. A combined database query has its own query plan; Python-level concurrency cannot be inferred from its SQL shape.
questions.Risk: Assuming stage concurrency understates latency. Conversely, parallelizing blindly can violate a shared database session's rules or increase load beyond intended limits.
questions.Trade: Sequential execution is easier to reason about with one session. Parallel execution may reduce latency for independent backends but requires separate safe resources, cancellation, and error policy.
questions.Try: Instrument start and finish events for both stages. Propose a parallel variant only after specifying which sessions and connections may be used concurrently.

questions.Q: When does a reranker help, and what can it not fix?
questions.A: A reranker reorders a candidate set using a more expensive relevance model, often evaluating the query and passage together. It helps distinguish closely related passages after a fast first-stage search. It cannot recover a document that never entered the candidate pool.
questions.Why: Hybrid retrieval accepts an optional Reranker protocol. a model-backed reranker is one adapter, while a host can supply another implementation. Typed responses preserve richer score information where required.
questions.Risk: External reranking may transmit document content to another provider, add latency, or fail. Authorization and data-handling policy must apply before transmission, and timeout or failure behavior should be explicit.
questions.Trade: Reranking spends more per candidate to improve final ordering. It may be unnecessary for exact identifier queries or small corpora with strong lexical matches.
questions.Try: Inspect ten candidates with similar vocabulary but different policy conditions. Compare fused ordering with reranked ordering and classify whether improvement justifies added cost.

questions.Q: How should query rewriting and multi-query retrieval be bounded?
questions.A: Query rewriting can make a conversational or ambiguous question more searchable; multi-query retrieval explores alternative phrasings. Both add work and can drift away from the original intent. Bounds should cover variant count, text length, time, and downstream calls.
questions.Why: A bounded query transformer wraps a host-provided transformer with limits and a timeout. Query generation should be an explicit optional dependency with measured cost and failure behavior.
questions.Risk: Generated variants may invent identifiers or broaden the scope of meaning. Scope filters must remain fixed across variants, and deduplication does not by itself calibrate rankings across all variants.
