questions.Why: Evidence assembly produces a stable bundle before a generator consumes it. The UI can show searching, assembling, generating, complete, cancelled, or failed states without pretending that partial text is a verified final answer.
questions.Risk: A network disconnect can leave server work running, and partial output may contain incomplete citation syntax. Propagate cancellation where possible and never silently mark a truncated stream complete.
questions.Trade: Early streaming improves perceived responsiveness while complicating error recovery and state handling. A non-streaming first version is easier to validate.
questions.Try: Design events for evidence_ready, answer_delta, complete, and failure. Simulate a disconnect after two deltas and specify what remains visible and retryable.

questions.Q: What should a useful RAG interface show besides the answer text?
questions.A: Show source titles and bounded excerpts, revision or freshness when relevant, citation navigation, loading and failure states, and a clear way to refine an ambiguous question. Make evidence accessible by keyboard and avoid presenting similarity as factual confidence.
questions.Why: The bundle already contains attribution and status data that a frontend can render. revision-aware source lookup provides a verification path when the user opens a citation; that path must retain the same identity and scope policy.
questions.Risk: Rendering document text as raw HTML can create cross-site scripting. Use safe text rendering or a deliberately sanitized markup pipeline, and treat citation URLs as untrusted input.
questions.Trade: More evidence improves transparency but can overwhelm users. Start with concise source summaries and progressive disclosure of full spans.
questions.Try: Build a search-only UI before chat. Include empty, stale, failed, and insufficient-budget examples, then test it entirely with keyboard navigation.

questions.Q: How should frontend state be separated from backend truth?
questions.A: Keep local interaction state such as expanded sources or draft input separate from server state such as operation status, evidence, and active document versions. Key cached results by the relevant identity, scope, query, and configuration or revision where necessary.
questions.Why: The retrieval service returns structured results, leaving the browser framework and caching library to the host. A frontend must preserve status distinctions and invalidate data when permissions or active generations change.
questions.Risk: Reusing a browser cache across sign-out or tenant switching can expose another user's evidence. Optimistically marking ingestion complete before activation can also misrepresent searchability.
questions.Trade: Explicit invalidation and cache partitioning add complexity but preserve correct user expectations. A simple no-cache first implementation can be preferable to unsafe reuse.
questions.Try: Switch tenants while a request is in flight. Ensure its late response cannot populate the new tenant's visible state or source drawer.

questions.Q: How should document upload and indexing progress be designed?
questions.A: Treat upload acceptance, source storage, extraction, embedding, activation, and searchability as distinct states. Persist the accepted source and enqueue background work according to the host's transaction policy. Return an operation identifier rather than blocking the request until every provider call completes.
questions.Why: Outbox and drainer interfaces decouple request latency from processing. Sync reports and events provide lifecycle information that a host can translate into progress, while active visibility determines when content can actually be searched.
questions.Risk: A successful upload can later fail extraction or embedding. The UI must not claim indexed status solely because bytes were received, and retry actions must avoid duplicate logical documents.
questions.Trade: Background workflows need polling or event delivery and durable state. Synchronous ingestion is simpler for small local experiments but less resilient under provider latency.
questions.Try: Define a document state machine from uploaded to searchable, with retry and failed states. Associate each transition with the component that can authoritatively report it.

questions.Q: What does production deployment require beyond installing optional extras?
questions.A: Provision durable stores and schemas, configure credentials and network access, run workers, set identity and permissions, select compatible profiles, validate startup, and establish backups, monitoring, and rollback. An optional dependency installs client code; it does not provision or secure its service.
questions.Why: The dependency manifest separates backend extras from dependency-free core, while health checks and integration examples help validate wiring. Actual database indexes and extension configuration remain deployment responsibilities.
questions.Risk: Multiple replicas using in-memory manifests or rate limits do not share authoritative state. Secrets in configuration fingerprints or public diagnostics can also create exposure.
questions.Trade: Managed services reduce some operations work and add cost or provider dependence. Self-hosting gives control and requires deeper operational expertise.
questions.Try: Produce a deployment inventory with ownership, persistence, backup, restart behavior, and secret source for every component. Include what happens when one replica restarts.

questions.Q: How would you plan capacity and handle overload?
questions.A: Model request arrival, per-stage service time, concurrency, queue capacity, database pools, and provider quotas. Apply admission control before expensive work, bound jobs, and shed optional processing when appropriate. Interactive search and batch ingestion should not starve each other accidentally.
questions.Why: The executor semaphore, transport limiter, job store, and health signals are local building blocks. The host must coordinate quotas across replicas and enforce end-to-end budgets.
questions.Risk: Increasing worker count can increase throttling rather than throughput. An unbounded backlog hides overload until memory, storage, or freshness collapses.
questions.Trade: Separate worker pools and queues improve isolation but add infrastructure. A shared small deployment is economical until contention becomes measurable.
questions.Try: Estimate sustainable throughput from provider concurrency and observed call duration, then load-test around that estimate. Report queue age as well as requests per second.

questions.Q: What portfolio project would demonstrate AI full-stack competence?
questions.A: Build a multi-tenant knowledge assistant with a search-first interface, revision-aware citations, background ingestion, a grounded answer policy, and a reproducible evaluation report. Show a failure and its diagnosis, not only a polished happy-path recording.
questions.Why: This combines frontend state, API design, identity, async jobs, data modeling, retrieval, generation, evaluation, and operations. the retrieval service provides the subsystem foundation while your work proves the application integration.
questions.Risk: A public demo can accidentally expose private sample documents or provider credentials. Use a reviewed fixture corpus and document implemented guarantees rather than aspirational architecture.
questions.Trade: A narrow reliable project is more convincing than many unfinished advanced features. Add reranking or multi-query only when your benchmark shows why they help.
questions.Try: Deliver a README with architecture, a threat-boundary map, benchmark results, three recovery demonstrations, and a five-minute walkthrough that opens a cited source revision.

questions.Q: How should I answer a senior system-design interview using this reference design?
questions.A: Start with requirements and constraints, then describe the offline and online flows, data identities, permission boundary, consistency model, failure recovery, quality evaluation, and capacity plan. Defend choices with case-based mechanisms and acknowledge which guarantees depend on host adapters.
questions.Why: The reference design's strongest lessons are explicit boundaries: prepare versus commit, candidates versus final evidence, logical visibility versus physical cleanup, and retrieval quality versus answer faithfulness. These distinctions scale beyond one library.
questions.Risk: Memorized pattern names and invented timing claims collapse under follow-up questions. Be ready to explain a crash interleaving, an authorization failure, and a measured quality trade-off in concrete terms.
questions.Trade: A good design is conditional on requirements. State when a keyword-only system, one transactional database, or a simpler synchronous workflow would be the better choice.
questions.Try: Give a 45-minute mock interview: five minutes requirements, ten architecture, ten consistency and security, ten evaluation and scale, and ten trade-offs and alternatives.

title: A reference AI application end to end
subtitle: Connect the reusable RAG library to the concrete the support platform backend.

questions.Q: What does a full support application add beyond a retrieval subsystem?
questions.A: A complete application adds authenticated APIs, customer-owned service requests, versioned knowledge, an agent runtime, confirmation workflows, persistent conversation history, background jobs, evaluation, and observability. Retrieval remains one service within that product.
questions.Why: Bind authenticated APIs, domain repositories, retrieval, model execution, and a client through typed contracts. Each layer should expose failures without pretending another layer has completed its work.
questions.Risk: Do not infer that every newer the retrieval service feature is integrated. The knowledge tool concatenates retrieved context directly; it does not automatically use the library's full an evidence assembler and revision-lookup contract.
questions.Trade: A narrow host binding is easier to ship, while richer evidence contracts add explicit statuses and provenance. Adoption requires wiring and migration rather than only upgrading a dependency.
questions.Try: Trace a question from the browser through authentication, tool selection, scoped retrieval, evidence assembly, generation, and source opening.

questions.Q: How should the orchestration framework be distinguished from model and retrieval adapters?
questions.A: The orchestration runtime controls the agent loop. A model adapter normalizes provider access, a retrieval service supplies evidence, and a tracing backend records execution. A product may use ADK, LangChain, or another runtime without changing these responsibilities.
questions.Why: Draw separate boxes for the runtime, model adapter, retrieval service, business services, and telemetry. Evaluate a replacement at its contract boundary rather than inferring responsibilities from package names.
questions.Risk: Framework confusion leads to examples that cannot run against the reference design's dependencies. The later LangChain, LangGraph, and A2A chapters explicitly describe alternatives or additions rather than pretending those frameworks are already installed.
questions.Trade: Staying with one orchestrator reduces state-model overlap. Adding another can solve a measured workflow need but introduces serialization, tracing, error, and deployment boundaries.
questions.Try: Make a dependency-layer table with web framework, agent runtime, model adapter, retrieval library, persistence layer, and tracing service. Name their concrete constructors.

questions.Q: How does an eligibility question differ from a request-status question?
questions.A: Coverage requires retrieving knowledge rules and applying a reviewed procedure to the user's facts. Claim status is a lookup of structured application state under the authenticated owner's scope. An answer about a policy is evidence-based interpretation; an answer about an existing request must reflect the actual recorded claim.
questions.Why: Route an exact request identifier to an authorized structured lookup. Route a knowledge question to applicable evidence. Evaluate both the intent decision and the resulting resource scope.
questions.Risk: Semantic similarity cannot establish that an arbitrary request ID belongs to the user or that a versioned rule applies to their contract. Tool-side identity checks remain necessary even when prompting selects the right tool.
questions.Trade: Separate tools make intent and authority clearer but require route-selection evaluation. One universal search tool is simpler and can blur exact facts with approximate matches.
questions.Try: Write expected tool sequences for an exact request ID, a remembered incident without an ID, and an eligibility question with missing facts.

questions.Q: What is the difference between an agent session and a conversation record?
questions.A: Agent sessions hold runtime state and events used by ADK. Conversation records hold application-visible messages, ownership, archival state, and IDs used by feedback and history APIs. They overlap in content but serve different contracts and lifecycle requirements.
questions.Why: Give runtime sessions and user-visible conversations separate identities and retention rules. Rehydrate only authorized history and reconcile message IDs with durable task and operation state.
questions.Risk: Divergence can replay a turn twice, omit tool results, or show UI messages that the agent cannot recall. Switching storage modes also needs a deliberate migration and restart story.
questions.Trade: Separate stores decouple product history from runtime implementation but require clear reconciliation and retention ownership. A single store reduces duplication and can bind the product tightly to one framework.
questions.Try: Trace which IDs identify the user, conversation, ADK session, invocation, user message, and assistant message. Explain which remain stable after a restart.

questions.Q: What is the real prepare-and-confirm boundary for request creation?
questions.A: Preparation validates fields and stores a pending submission with a confirmation token and expiry. Confirmation is an authenticated API operation that locks the pending submission, creates the service request and associated records, marks completion, and commits. Agent prose does not itself complete the financial workflow.
questions.Why: Prepare validated intent, present exact parameters for review, then verify approval inside a short transaction. Persist the authoritative result before claiming the action completed.
questions.Risk: The prompt's phrase that a tool call is the confirmation action can be misunderstood. The actual database submission still requires the separate route. A textual yes from the model is not proof that the API operation succeeded.
questions.Trade: Two steps add user interaction and pending-state management while reducing accidental writes. A one-step workflow is faster but gives less opportunity to review material fields.
questions.Try: Follow one token from preparation to a locked confirmation transaction. Identify which operation first makes the service request durable.

questions.Q: Why separate policy procedures from knowledge facts?
questions.A: A procedure describes how to investigate a question or route an unclear request. A knowledge source supplies actual limits, deductibles, exclusions, and conditions. The procedure should not become an alternative authority for contractual facts merely because it is easier to retrieve.
questions.Why: Store playbooks as workflow guidance and knowledge articles as factual authority. Version both and evaluate whether a current procedure can still select an inapplicable source.
questions.Risk: A stale procedure can direct an incomplete investigation, while a current procedure can still be combined with the wrong rule revision. Both source identities need to be visible in evaluation and operational diagnosis.
questions.Trade: Separating reasoning guidance from factual material supports independent review but adds retrieval calls and version combinations. Hardcoding all instructions in one prompt is easier to start and harder to govern.
questions.Try: Label every sentence in the eligibility-review playbook as a workflow rule or factual claim. Move any unsupported numeric policy claim back to the authoritative source layer.

questions.Q: Where does eventual consistency appear to a customer?
questions.A: A request can be durably submitted before its embedding job completes, so exact structured lookup and semantic search may temporarily disagree. Notification delivery can also lag the request transaction. These are different read and delivery projections of one business operation.
questions.Why: Commit the request and its downstream jobs together. Serve exact status from authoritative records while exposing indexing or notification lag as separate projection states.
questions.Risk: A search miss immediately after filing must not be reported as proof that no claim exists. An authoritative exact lookup can confirm persistence while the index catches up.
questions.Trade: Asynchronous processing keeps submission independent of provider latency but introduces lag and recovery work. Synchronous indexing is simpler conceptually and couples business availability to model services.
questions.Try: Pause the embedding worker, file a service request, and compare exact lookup with semantic search. Define the appropriate user-visible status for each result.

questions.Q: What are the main trust boundaries in this application?
questions.A: Boundaries include browser-to-API identity, model-to-tool authority, source-to-prompt content, application-to-database privileges, application-to-model disclosure, and application-to-observability export. Each boundary has a different actor and failure mode.
questions.Why: Annotate every edge with identity, allowed data, and permitted effects. Model output, retrieved text, remote metadata, and observability exports cross different trust boundaries.
questions.Risk: A protected chat endpoint is insufficient if a tool trusts model-supplied owner IDs or a trace exports private claim text. Read and write paths require separate evidence of enforcement.
questions.Trade: Explicit boundaries add policy and testing effort but make failures diagnosable. Combining all access behind a powerful agent credential simplifies integration and magnifies mistakes.
questions.Try: Draw the support runtime diagram and annotate every edge with identity, permitted data, and whether the receiver can initiate authoritative writes.

questions.Q: Which application guarantees must be established end to end?
questions.A: Implemented mechanisms include owner-scoped case retrieval, a locked confirmation row, caller-owned submission transactions, typed streaming events, optional shared idempotency, and trace instrumentation. Their deployment guarantees depend on real database behavior, chosen storage settings, provider configuration, and complete use of the intended paths.
questions.Why: Define tool availability, ownership checks, approval validation, persistence, and stream outcomes as independently testable contracts. A framework swap should preserve or explicitly revise those contracts.
questions.Risk: Reading a comment about deployment defaults or a role model as proof of configured behavior creates false confidence. Follow defaults and call sites rather than naming available classes.
questions.Trade: Conservative defaults support local development but may require production gates. Rejecting startup on missing critical state is stricter than silently falling back to local state.
questions.Try: Create a deployment evidence checklist showing the selected session, idempotency, rate-limit, and tracing backends without printing secrets.

questions.Q: How should you trace a request across the complete application?
questions.A: Start at user intent and verified identity, follow tool selection and scoped services, inspect evidence and model output, then confirm persisted results and client state. Trace the actual path, including failures and recovery.
questions.Why: Turn architectural guarantees into acceptance tests. A diagram describes intended responsibilities; concurrent workers, deployment settings, provider errors, and bypass paths determine whether the implementation actually meets them.
questions.Risk: A diagram can describe an ideal design while a bypass path violates it. Verify each critical boundary through observable behavior rather than relying only on intended structure.
questions.Trade: Cross-project tracing takes more effort than a single overview but teaches integration judgment, the central skill in full-stack AI engineering.
questions.Try: Trace three synthetic tasks: a factual answer, an approved write, and a provider failure. Record the invariant checked at every boundary.

title: Relational data modeling and migrations
subtitle: Learn why the application needs more than a vector index.

questions.Q: Why store support service requests in relational tables instead of only vector documents?
questions.A: Service requests have exact ownership, monetary amounts, lifecycle states, references, and transaction boundaries. A vector index optimizes similarity retrieval and does not replace those relational invariants. The same request can have an authoritative row and a derived search representation.
questions.Why: Keep authoritative ownership, state transitions, and relationships in constrained transactional records. Use vector indexes as derived search projections that can be rebuilt, not as the only source of business truth.
questions.Risk: Treating the vector record as the sole source of truth makes exact authorization, status transitions, and recovery dependent on a derived index. Search ranking cannot decide whether a service request exists or who owns it.
questions.Trade: Relational plus search modeling creates projection maintenance work but supports exact operations and flexible discovery. A text-only prototype is smaller and insufficient for authoritative workflows.
questions.Try: Mark every Claim column as identity, business fact, authority constraint, lifecycle metadata, or derived search data. Explain which can be rebuilt.

questions.Q: Why have both a UUID primary key and a human-readable request ID?
questions.A: A UUID provides an internal identifier suitable for references; a separate request ID provides a support-friendly external label. They have different display and collision properties. Neither identifier should be treated as an authorization secret.
questions.Why: Choose immutable internal identifiers and stable public references deliberately. Scope uniqueness to the right tenant or operation and reject collisions through database constraints.
questions.Risk: Shortened random identifiers can collide. A production collision-handling path should distinguish a retryable uniqueness conflict from unrelated database errors, and users must still be scoped even when an ID is known.
questions.Trade: Friendly IDs improve support and communication while adding an extra index and identity mapping. Full opaque IDs are simpler but awkward to read aloud.
questions.Try: Explain how an identifier collision differs from an idempotent replay. Design a bounded generation retry that does not duplicate a pending submission.

questions.Q: Why use Numeric and Decimal for request amounts?
questions.A: Decimal arithmetic and a fixed-scale Numeric column represent monetary values more predictably than binary floating point. Currency precision, rounding, allowed scale, and upper bounds are part of the domain contract rather than formatting details.
questions.Why: Use decimal representations and explicit currency rules. Validate scale and range before persistence, and preserve decimal strings across API serialization rather than round-tripping through binary floats.
questions.Risk: A Decimal column cannot retroactively undo precision lost earlier in JSON parsing, float conversion, or arithmetic. Validation and serialization must preserve the intended amount end to end.
questions.Trade: Decimal values need explicit JSON handling and careful provider-tool schemas. Float is convenient for generic numeric tools but weakens exact-money guarantees.
questions.Try: Trace an amount with cents from browser JSON through Pydantic, pending JSONB, confirmation, and SQL storage. Propose a Decimal-preserving signature and matching tests.

questions.Q: How do foreign keys, unique constraints, and check constraints complement application validation?
questions.A: Application validation gives useful error messages; database constraints protect against every writer sharing the database. Foreign keys preserve references, unique constraints enforce identity rules, and check constraints reject invalid row-level values even when a route is bypassed.
questions.Why: Specify foreign keys, nullability, uniqueness, and state checks in migrations. Application validation improves errors; database constraints protect against concurrent callers and alternative write paths.
questions.Risk: Assuming all invariants are enforced because ORM types exist leaves gaps for scripts, workers, and future routes. Constraints also need deliberate delete and migration behavior.
questions.Trade: Strong constraints simplify consistency reasoning but can complicate staged migrations and bulk imports. Relaxing them requires another proven enforcement mechanism.
questions.Try: Compare the Claim, PendingRequest, an indexing job, and a request event models with their migrations. List invariants enforced only in Python and those enforced by PostgreSQL.

questions.Q: What belongs in normalized columns versus JSONB?
questions.A: Put fields used for relationships, strict constraints, frequent filtering, and stable reporting in typed columns. JSONB is useful for variable event payloads or a prepared-form snapshot. Its flexibility does not remove the need for schema versions, validation, or selective indexing.
questions.Why: Normalize identity, ownership, status, amounts, timestamps, and relationships that need constraints. Reserve JSONB for evolving payloads whose validation and query needs are explicitly managed.
questions.Risk: Unversioned JSON can become unreadable after schema changes. Copying an entire stale state blob can also overwrite concurrent updates, while arbitrary JSON may retain more private data than needed.
questions.Trade: JSONB speeds evolving payloads and weakens some relational guarantees. Normalize stable, high-value fields instead of treating the database as a dictionary with no contracts.
questions.Try: Design a version field and migration reader for a prepared submission whose incident_date field was added later. Explain the fallback for older records.

questions.Q: Why does the owner-and-created-at composite index matter?
questions.A: A request list filters by owner and orders by creation time. An index beginning with owner_id and then created_at can support that access pattern more directly than two unrelated indexes. Index design should follow real predicates, ordering, and pagination.
questions.Why: Start index design from actual predicates and ordering. Inspect query plans and representative data distributions, then balance faster reads against write cost and maintenance.
questions.Risk: An index declaration does not prove an efficient plan at production data sizes. Additional sort keys, selective predicates, and row estimates can change the plan; unused indexes still cost writes and storage.
questions.Trade: More indexes accelerate selected reads while slowing mutation and increasing maintenance. Validate with representative EXPLAIN plans rather than indexing every column reflexively.
questions.Try: Compare the owner-scoped listing plan with and without the composite index in a disposable database. Include a tie-breaking ID if you design keyset pagination.

questions.Q: How do knowledge versions differ from active knowledge chunks?
questions.A: A knowledge version records the source and indexing configuration over time. Policy chunks are searchable material for a version. Keeping version records does not necessarily mean every historical chunk remains retained or that a query selects the contract applicable to an incident.
questions.Why: Track effective intervals separately from indexing time. Resolve the applicable source revision before searching its derived chunks, and retain the revision needed to verify an earlier answer.
questions.Risk: Current-source retrieval can answer the wrong historical question even when its text is accurately quoted. Historical evidence needs both retention and an explicit applicable-version filter.
questions.Trade: Retaining every version supports audits and costs storage and selection logic. Current-only indexing is simpler and must state its scope honestly.
questions.Try: Create two rule revisions with different deductibles and one incident between their effective dates. Define the query and citation fields required to choose correctly.

questions.Q: Why use Alembic migrations instead of create_all for production evolution?
questions.A: Create_all creates missing schema objects represented in current metadata; it is not a reviewed sequence for changing existing columns, backfilling data, or coordinating old and new application versions. Migrations record explicit upgrade steps and dependencies.
questions.Why: Make production schema changes explicit and reviewed. Assign migration ownership, verify upgrades against existing data, and coordinate application compatibility instead of relying on runtime table creation.
questions.Risk: Runtime-created tables can escape a migration policy, and concurrent DDL can disrupt startup. Inventory every schema owner and make a failed migration visibly block incompatible application use.
questions.Trade: Migrations add review and deployment sequencing but make history inspectable. Runtime creation is convenient for framework state and harder to govern consistently.
questions.Try: Define which component owns each reference table and write a reviewed upgrade path for an existing populated database.

questions.Q: What is an expand-and-contract migration?
questions.A: Add a compatible schema surface first, deploy code that can read old and new forms, backfill safely, switch writers, then remove the old form in a later release. The sequence allows rolling deployment and rollback without requiring every process to switch simultaneously.
questions.Why: Add a compatible new structure, backfill with bounded work, deploy readers and writers deliberately, and remove obsolete structure only after verifying all consumers have migrated.
questions.Risk: A backfill can hold locks or overload the database; a destructive cleanup can make application rollback impossible. Background jobs may also contain payloads written by an older schema version.
questions.Trade: Compatibility periods increase temporary complexity and reduce deployment coupling. A single destructive migration is shorter and can require a maintenance window.
questions.Try: Design a migration from float-shaped tool input to explicit decimal-string amounts. Include old pending submissions and jobs, not just current Claim rows.

questions.Q: How should you model authoritative events versus derived projections?
questions.A: A request event records lifecycle history; a request status is a current-state projection. Embedding records and notifications are downstream projections. Agent session events describe runtime execution, while audit events describe selected high-value actions. These logs are related but not interchangeable event-sourcing systems.
questions.Why: Separate authoritative lifecycle records from derived search and notification projections. Define replay and reconciliation for each projection rather than calling every append-only table an event-sourced system.
questions.Risk: Calling any append-only table event sourcing overstates replayability. A complete event-sourced design needs sufficient immutable events, deterministic projection rebuilding, versioning, and a declared source of truth.
questions.Trade: Current rows plus a transition trail provide useful history with lower complexity. Full event sourcing improves replay options and adds substantial schema and operational obligations.
questions.Try: For each event table, state whether it can rebuild a Claim exactly. Identify missing facts before claiming replay-based recovery.

title: Transactions, locks, and concurrency
subtitle: Prove what happens when retries, users, and workers race.

questions.Q: How does SELECT FOR UPDATE prevent duplicate confirmation?
questions.A: Confirmation locks the pending submission selected by token, owner, and pending status. A second transaction targeting the same row waits; after the first commits, the second must observe the updated state under the actual isolation rules. The lock protects a database transition, not the browser button.
questions.Why: Select the pending operation by trusted owner and token, acquire the appropriate row lock, recheck expiry and state, then apply the effect and final state in one transaction.
questions.Risk: An internal commit would release the lock before the pending row changes, enabling duplicate creation. A request timeout or double click is expected behavior to test, not evidence that the client will never retry.
questions.Trade: Pessimistic locking simplifies this contested transition but makes lock duration important. Keep remote model work out of the locked transaction.
questions.Try: Start two confirmations simultaneously in separate database sessions. Assert one logical claim and one consumed submission, then inspect the losing request's result.

questions.Q: What is the difference between flush, commit, and rollback?
questions.A: Flush sends pending ORM changes to the transaction, allowing generated identities and database constraints to be observed. Commit makes the transaction's successful changes durable. Rollback discards its transactional changes. Flushed data is not therefore committed, and another session's visibility depends on isolation.
questions.Why: Flush exposes transactional changes and constraint errors without committing. Keep one owner for commit and rollback so nested services cannot partially finalize a larger business operation.
questions.Risk: Catching a database exception and continuing with the same failed transaction can produce further errors. A swallowed exception is not a successful recovery; rollback or a correctly scoped savepoint is needed.
questions.Trade: Caller-owned transactions permit atomic composition but require explicit ownership. Helpers that commit themselves are easier in isolation and unsafe inside larger workflows.
questions.Try: Inject failure after the service request flush but before the final commit. Inspect all related tables from another session after rollback.

questions.Q: What does PostgreSQL Read Committed mean for an application workflow?
questions.A: Ordinary statements see committed state as of each statement's snapshot, so two reads in one transaction can observe intervening commits. A transaction boundary alone does not make a sequence of business decisions appear serial. Locking or conditional updates must protect the relevant invariant.
questions.Why: Under Read Committed, separate statements may observe different committed snapshots. Protect a multi-statement invariant with appropriate constraints, locks, or guarded updates instead of assuming one stable view.
questions.Risk: A pattern that reads pending, calls external work, then updates completed can race under ordinary concurrency. Shared data snapshots and write authority are different properties.
questions.Trade: Stronger isolation can reduce anomalies while increasing retries and contention. It does not eliminate the need for idempotent external effects.
questions.Try: Reproduce a changing read in two sessions, then compare a locked confirmation and a conditional UPDATE. Record actual transaction settings.

questions.Q: When would optimistic concurrency control be useful?
questions.A: Optimistic control updates a row only when its version or prior state matches what the caller observed. A zero-row update signals a conflict. It suits edits where collisions are uncommon and a caller can reload rather than hold a lock during long user interaction.
questions.Why: Include the expected version in the update predicate and require exactly one affected row. On conflict, reload state and revalidate intent before deciding whether retry is safe.
questions.Risk: Checking a version in Python and then issuing an unconditional update is not optimistic concurrency control. The comparison and mutation must be one database operation.
questions.Trade: Short conditional writes reduce waiting but require conflict handling. Row locks can be simpler for a small critical transition with many related writes.
questions.Try: Write a versioned update for a hypothetical claim note. Make two editors submit the same expected version and verify only one succeeds.

questions.Q: How does job selection differ from durable job ownership?
questions.A: A selection transaction can return candidate IDs and then release its locks. If acquisition happens later, a guarded update and its returned rows establish which worker owns each job. Alternatively, select and claim atomically in one transaction. Inspect the full lifecycle before asserting exclusive ownership.
questions.Why: If candidate selection ends its transaction before acquisition, a later conditional update establishes ownership. Alternatively, claim atomically in one transaction; inspect the whole lifecycle before asserting exclusivity.
questions.Risk: Describing selection alone as exclusive ownership hides a race and encourages unsafe future changes. Completion and reclamation also need ownership-aware conditions to prevent obsolete workers from overwriting newer outcomes.
questions.Trade: Split selection and guarded claiming compose with the generic protocol but require more careful reasoning. One atomic claim statement can simplify the implementation at the cost of adapter-specific SQL.
questions.Try: Interleave two workers between selection and marking. Verify the loser receives no processing payload for the contested job.

questions.Q: Why is one AsyncSession per concurrent task important?
questions.A: AsyncSession represents mutable transactional and ORM state. Independent concurrent operations should use independent sessions rather than sharing one session inside asyncio.gather. An async driver does not make one transaction object safe for arbitrary concurrent use.
questions.Why: Create an independent AsyncSession per independently concurrent transaction. Bound database concurrency separately from provider calls and avoid sharing mutable ORM state across unrelated async tasks.
questions.Risk: Sharing can cause state errors, unintended transaction coupling, or unpredictable query sequencing. Creating too many sessions instead can exhaust the pool, so concurrency also needs a bound.
questions.Trade: Separate sessions allow independent I/O while consuming additional connections and potentially observing different snapshots. Sequential queries on one session are easier when one consistent transaction is required.
questions.Try: Compare concurrent reads with separate sessions and sequential reads with one session. Measure pool checkout waits and document the required consistency model.

questions.Q: Can persistent ADK session state still suffer lost updates?
questions.A: Yes. Persistence retains state but does not automatically merge concurrent updates. If two workers read one version, modify different fields, and overwrite the whole JSON object, the later write can discard the earlier change.
questions.Why: Choose session serialization, optimistic versions, or explicit field-level merge semantics. Test two stale readers changing different fields; durable storage alone does not protect against a lost update.
questions.Risk: An append-only event record can survive while the latest state loses another turn's field. Sequence numbers also do not prove the model saw a serial conversational history.
questions.Trade: Per-session turn serialization improves consistency and reduces same-conversation throughput. Delta updates or optimistic versions offer alternatives with their own conflict policy.
questions.Try: Load the same session twice, apply different state keys concurrently, and inspect both the event log and final state.

questions.Q: Why is the Redis idempotency claim a best-effort mechanism rather than exactly-once execution?
questions.A: The claim has a finite TTL, waiters stop waiting after a bounded time, and Redis outages permit local execution. A slow winner can still run while another replica gives up and recomputes. The claim value is not a durable operation result or a fencing token for a business write.
questions.Why: A short-lived Redis lease can reduce duplicate model work while expiring during a slow call. Use an owner token with checked release, and enforce business idempotency through a durable operation key in the authoritative database.
questions.Risk: An obsolete worker can delete or overwrite a newer lease if ownership is not checked. Duplicate model calls may add cost; repeated business writes require a separate durable protection.
questions.Trade: Best-effort deduplication improves responsiveness. Stronger operation state requires ownership tokens, durable result identity, and explicit timeout/retry semantics.
questions.Try: Make a model turn outlast the service request TTL and waiter deadline. Count model executions separately from durable business effects.

questions.Q: How should deadlocks, lock timeouts, and serialization failures be handled?
questions.A: Acquire shared resources in a consistent order, keep transactions short, bound waiting, and retry only the whole appropriate transactional unit when the database reports a retryable conflict. Reusing a partially failed session or blindly retrying external effects is unsafe.
questions.Why: Classify database errors and retry only an entire safely repeatable transaction under a bounded deadline. Preserve the business operation key and avoid retrying partial side effects blindly.
questions.Risk: Retrying a transaction can repeat already-sent emails or model calls if they occur inside the unit. Outbox writes let the database retry without repeating external delivery synchronously.
questions.Trade: Retries improve recovery while increasing tail latency. An overloaded system needs admission control, not only more retry attempts.
questions.Try: Create a two-row opposite-order locking exercise in a disposable database. Record the failure class and retry the complete unit with a bounded policy.

questions.Q: How do you test concurrency without relying on random sleeps?
questions.A: Use controlled barriers or events to pause workers at known boundaries, then force a specific interleaving. Assert durable state and ownership outcomes, not only response codes. Use a real PostgreSQL instance for lock and isolation service requests.
questions.Why: Use barriers or explicit synchronization to control the interleaving. Assert final rows and operation outcomes after takeover, duplicate confirmation, deadlock recovery, and stale-worker completion attempts.
questions.Risk: A test that runs two coroutines on one session may test an invalid integration rather than a real race. An in-memory SQLite database cannot establish PostgreSQL row-lock semantics.
questions.Trade: Deterministic integration tests take setup but produce stronger evidence and fewer flaky timing assumptions. Broad stress tests complement them and do not replace them.
questions.Try: Specify barriers for two confirmations, two job service requests, and two session-state updates. State the invariant each test could falsify.

title: Securing database operations
subtitle: Constrain credentials, queries, disclosure, and recovery—not only SQL strings.

questions.Q: What does least privilege mean for application, migration, and reporting database roles?
questions.A: Use separate credentials for runtime queries, schema migration, and analysis. The application role should have only the tables and operations its workload needs; it should not need unrestricted DDL or superuser access. Read-only reporting still needs row and data-disclosure controls.
questions.Why: Provision separate application, migration, reporting, and worker roles. Verify actual grants and keep credentials outside model context; sharing one connection string does not establish least privilege.
questions.Risk: A single powerful credential turns a query injection, tool bug, or compromised worker into a broader database incident. A model must never receive that credential or arbitrary SQL authority.
questions.Trade: Separate roles require grants and migration coordination but reduce blast radius. One admin credential is convenient locally and inappropriate as evidence of production isolation.
questions.Try: Design a grant matrix for API, embedding worker, notification worker, migrator, and analyst. Include which sensitive tables each must never read.

questions.Q: How could PostgreSQL Row-Level Security complement owner-scoped queries?
questions.A: RLS applies database policies to rows readable or writable through a role. It can add a second barrier when an application query forgets owner filtering. Its protection depends on actual role grants, bypass behavior, identity propagation, and tested policies.
questions.Why: Enable and test RLS under the actual non-bypass role. Bind identity transaction-locally, verify pooled connection reuse, and understand owner or administrative bypass behavior.
questions.Risk: Table owners or privileged roles can bypass knowledge rules under documented conditions. Connection reuse can leak session-level identity if it is not reset; transaction-local settings and pool tests matter.
questions.Trade: Database enforcement strengthens defense in depth but complicates jobs, migrations, tests, and administrative workflows. It does not replace server authentication.
questions.Try: In a disposable schema, create a transaction-local owner setting and policy. Test two users through reused pooled connections and verify writes as well as reads.

questions.Q: Why are parameterized values insufficient for arbitrary query generation?
questions.A: Binding values prevents them from being interpreted as SQL syntax in the intended parameter position. It does not make arbitrary table names, operators, SQL fragments, or model-generated statements safe. Query structure needs a trusted construction path and an allowlisted operation surface.
questions.Why: Parameterize values and allowlist identifiers, operators, and query shapes. Arbitrary generated SQL remains a privilege boundary even when some values use bound parameters.
questions.Risk: An LLM-generated SELECT can still disclose unauthorized rows, invoke expensive functions, or exploit permissions even if it contains no classic string-concatenation injection.
questions.Trade: Narrow domain tools limit exploratory flexibility and support predictable authorization. A natural-language analytics feature needs an independently constrained read model and query policy.
questions.Try: Design an exact aggregate tool for a user's service requests using typed inputs. Explain why it is safer than giving the model a raw database connection.

questions.Q: How do database credentials and TLS fit into the trust model?
questions.A: Credentials authenticate a process to the database; TLS protects transport and can verify server identity. Neither automatically limits which rows the process may read. Rotate credentials, use appropriate secret storage, and validate certificate settings in the actual deployment.
questions.Why: Verify server identity through the configured TLS policy, rotate credentials, and restrict network access. A reachable encrypted connection still needs resource authorization and least privilege.
questions.Risk: Printing URLs or raw driver errors can expose passwords or infrastructure details. Copying secrets into model context, traces, sample files, or shell arguments creates additional disclosure paths.
questions.Trade: Managed identities or short-lived credentials reduce secret lifetime where supported, while adding integration requirements. Static credentials are simpler and need deliberate rotation and incident response.
questions.Try: Create a secret-free deployment evidence record showing connection identity, TLS verification mode, role grants, and rotation ownership. Do not include the secret value.

questions.Q: Which timeouts protect database availability?
questions.A: Bound pool checkout, connection establishment, statement execution, lock waits, and idle transactions according to the workload. These limits solve different problems. An HTTP timeout alone may leave server-side queries or open transactions consuming resources.
questions.Why: Set connection, statement, lock, and transaction-duration limits according to workload. Cancel abandoned work and keep application deadlines shorter than an uncontrolled sequence of downstream waits.
questions.Risk: An expensive permitted query can be a denial-of-service vector. Very short timeouts can also cause retry amplification or repeatedly abort useful work.
questions.Trade: Tighter limits improve isolation and can reduce completion rates. Use separate knowledge rules for interactive search, migrations, and backfills instead of one global number.
questions.Try: Propose settings for pool wait, lock wait, and statement time with a measured request budget. Simulate a blocked transaction and observe rollback and connection reuse.

questions.Q: What is the difference between secure deletion, logical revocation, and retention?
questions.A: Revocation stops authorized disclosure. Logical deletion changes application visibility. Physical deletion removes stored copies, subject to backups and retention. Service records, embeddings, pending payloads, conversations, traces, and notifications can each retain different copies of the same private facts.
questions.Why: Distinguish removing search visibility from deleting retained originals, embeddings, caches, logs, and backups. Define which lifecycle obligation applies to every derived artifact.
questions.Risk: Deleting a relational row may leave vectors, trace payloads, exports, or historical messages accessible. Conversely, deleting everything indiscriminately can violate a required evidence-retention policy; the applicable policy must be established outside this engineering guide.
questions.Trade: Purpose-specific retention minimizes unnecessary copies while preserving required records. One indefinite retention setting is easy and accumulates disclosure risk.
questions.Try: Draw a data inventory for a single claim description and specify revocation, retention, deletion, and verification owners for every copy.

questions.Q: Is an append-only audit table automatically tamper-proof and complete?
questions.A: No. Append-only is an application behavior unless database privileges and external retention enforce it. Completeness depends on what is recorded and what happens when recording fails. Trace data and business audit records also have different reliability requirements.
questions.Why: Give required audit events transactional or explicitly durable delivery semantics. Append-only application behavior does not prevent privileged database changes, and a failed transaction needs rollback or a savepoint.
questions.Risk: A missing trail can matter during an investigation. Also, swallowing a failed SQL statement does not by itself restore a PostgreSQL transaction; savepoint and rollback behavior require testing.
questions.Trade: Best-effort audit favors availability. Mandatory audit or a transactional audit outbox provides stronger completeness at the cost of possible business-operation failure or more infrastructure.
questions.Try: Inject an audit insertion failure and inspect the surrounding transaction. Define which actions must fail closed if audit cannot be guaranteed.

questions.Q: How should backup and point-in-time recovery be tested for an AI application?
questions.A: Restore the relational database and verify business records, ownership, migrations, outbox state, and knowledge versions. Then decide whether vector projections should be restored or rebuilt. The recovery objective concerns a coherent application state, not only a successful backup command.
questions.Why: Restore a known fixture into an isolated environment and verify authoritative records, outbox work, derived indexes, credentials, and access policy. Measure recovery time and actual recoverable data loss.
questions.Risk: Replaying old notification or submission jobs can duplicate effects. A backup also contains private data and requires its own encryption, access, and retention policy.
questions.Trade: Rebuilding vectors reduces backup coupling and takes time and provider cost. Snapshotting every projection can accelerate recovery while making consistency coordination harder.
questions.Try: Write a restore drill with a known claim, pending job, rule revision, and revoked user. Verify exact reads, search visibility, and safe job resumption.

questions.Q: Why separate operational metrics from database content exports?
questions.A: Counts, durations, and sanitized error categories support capacity and health without automatically exporting claim text, customer identifiers, or confirmation tokens. Content exports need an explicit purpose and access policy rather than being a side effect of debugging.
questions.Why: Export allowlisted operational metadata instead of whole records. Separate observability access from business-data access and review whether identifiers themselves reveal sensitive relationships.
questions.Risk: A credential-safe SQL logger can still expose PII through parameter values. Traces may be readable by a broader audience than the application database.
questions.Trade: Minimal telemetry reduces diagnosis detail; controlled replay fixtures and opt-in redacted samples can provide useful debugging with less disclosure.
questions.Try: Trace one claim description and token through logs, tool spans, model callbacks, and telemetry endpoints. Record exactly what leaves the process.

questions.Q: How should database security be verified before adding agent autonomy?
questions.A: Prove owner filtering, least-privilege credentials, constrained tools, input validation, timeout behavior, audit policy, and recovery using the actual storage setup. A more autonomous planner increases the number and variety of operations, so it should inherit a secure capability surface rather than broadening it.
questions.Why: Test with the real application role and cross-tenant fixtures. Exercise denied reads and writes, pooled reuse, arbitrary-input rejection, backup access, and every non-agent administrative path.
questions.Risk: A framework demo may call internal functions directly and skip route dependencies. The same tool needs an identity context or service principal appropriate to its execution path.
questions.Trade: A capability-oriented service layer takes design work and supports safe reuse across orchestration frameworks. Direct ORM access inside every agent is fast to prototype and hard to govern.
questions.Try: Build a deny-first test matrix for interactive users, background workers, and remote agents. Include actions each principal may read, prepare, confirm, or never perform.

title: API identity and application security
subtitle: Carry trusted user identity through routes, tools, workers, and streams.

questions.Q: How are JWTs validated and converted into database ownership?
questions.A: Validate the token under an explicit issuer, audience, algorithm, and lifetime profile, resolve the subject to a trusted application principal, and authorize access to each resource. A model-generated owner identifier cannot replace authenticated identity.
questions.Why: Validate signature, allowed algorithm, issuer, audience, expiry, and required claims under the token profile. Resolve the trusted principal and enforce resource ownership in services, not model arguments.
questions.Risk: A valid token may remain usable after access should be revoked unless the product checks revocation or session versions. Choose lifetime and refresh behavior from the threat model.
questions.Trade: Stateless token checks scale well, while immediate revocation needs additional state or shorter-lived credentials. Database user lookup already provides one current-state validation point.
questions.Try: Test expired, malformed, deleted-user, wrong-signature, and valid tokens. Verify that a known request ID still requires owner authorization.

questions.Q: Why are HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, CORS, and CSRF different controls?
questions.A: HttpOnly limits script access to cookies, Secure limits cookie transport to HTTPS, and SameSite constrains some cross-site sending. CORS controls browser access across origins. CSRF protection addresses unwanted state-changing requests made with ambient credentials. None is interchangeable with user authorization.
questions.Why: Set cookie and origin policies explicitly for the deployment. Review state-changing routes for CSRF and XSS exposure; CORS, SameSite, HttpOnly, and Secure address different browser behaviors.
questions.Risk: These settings do not establish a complete CSRF review of all mutations and deployment origins. XSS can still issue authorized actions even when it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie.
questions.Trade: Cookie authentication simplifies browser sessions but requires deliberate origin and state-change policy. Bearer clients have different storage and transport concerns.
questions.Try: Build a matrix for sign-in, confirmation, cancellation, and logout across trusted and untrusted origins. State which server-side checks enforce each result.

questions.Q: How does ContextVar prevent cross-request identity leakage?
questions.A: ContextVar associates a value with an asynchronous execution context rather than one mutable process-global variable. Concurrent requests can therefore carry different identities through await boundaries. It is a context propagation mechanism, not an authorization decision or durable identity store.
questions.Why: Bind task-local identity at the authenticated boundary and reset it in a finally block. A background task must receive a deliberate identity rather than rely on accidental inherited context.
questions.Risk: Capturing context for a task that outlives a request can retain stale identity. Failing to reset temporary bindings can also confuse tests or reused execution contexts. Server code must define where identity begins and ends.
questions.Trade: Implicit context reduces parameter threading and can hide dependencies. Explicit identity parameters improve local clarity and require more signatures.
questions.Try: Run two concurrent tool calls under separate context bindings. Test missing identity and an outliving background task; verify both fail or receive an explicit service identity as intended.

questions.Q: Why must case ownership be checked in tools as well as routes?
questions.A: Agent tools may execute through a runner, test harness, or future remote protocol without passing through a particular HTTP route. A protected route cannot be the only place a domain operation learns whose data it may access.
questions.Why: Authorize the resource inside the service called by every adapter. A protected chat endpoint cannot make a later model-selected identifier trustworthy.
questions.Risk: A model-supplied user_id is untrusted even if it is a valid UUID. A future LangChain adapter must not expose that internal parameter as a tool argument the model can freely choose.
questions.Trade: Repeated enforcement at domain boundaries adds code and protects alternate callers. Duplicated policy implementations can drift, so centralize shared service authorization where possible.
questions.Try: Invoke the service request-search tool directly without an HTTP request and with the wrong user context. Verify that knowing another user's request ID does not reveal it.

questions.Q: What is the distinction between RBAC and resource ownership here?
questions.A: Role-Based Access Control determines whether a principal may perform a category of action; ownership determines which records that principal may affect. A support operator role does not automatically justify unrestricted access to every customer's service requests.
questions.Why: Use roles for permitted categories of action and ownership for access to a particular resource. Check both when a privileged operation also targets tenant-scoped data.
questions.Risk: Replacing the allowlist with a broad role check without resource policy can overgrant authority. Tests that widen the allowlist for fixtures do not prove production administration is configured.
questions.Trade: Combining role and attribute checks is more expressive and more complex. A deny-by-default seam is safer than silently pretending a missing administrative policy exists.
questions.Try: Define reader, customer, handler, and administrator actions with both role and record-scope rules. Map each rule to its actual enforcement point.

questions.Q: Why does password hashing require more than naming Argon2?
questions.A: A password hash uses intentionally costly computation and salt to resist offline guessing. Operational parameters, input limits, verification errors, rehash policy, and login rate limiting matter too. A hash algorithm name alone does not establish timing-safe user enumeration resistance.
questions.Why: Use a valid dummy hash with a reviewed work factor for unknown accounts. Compare timing distributions under load and keep authentication errors consistent without suppressing operational diagnostics.
questions.Risk: Malformed dummy verification can return faster than a real check. Unbounded password input or excessive concurrent hashing can also consume resources before the agent is involved.
questions.Trade: Higher hashing cost protects stolen hashes and increases authentication resource use. Choose measured parameters and a valid equivalent dummy path.
questions.Try: Benchmark known-user wrong-password and unknown-user checks with reviewed test data. Verify hash validity and compare distributions without asserting perfect constant time.

questions.Q: How should confirmation tokens be treated as capabilities?
questions.A: A confirmation token identifies a specific prepared action and should be bound to the user, payload, pending state, and expiry. Possession alone should not bypass authentication. Material edits should produce a new reviewed operation and invalidate or supersede the old one server-side.
questions.Why: Bind confirmation to owner, exact parameters, revision, expiry, and pending state. Supersede earlier approvals explicitly after material changes and reject reused completed tokens.
questions.Risk: A model's statement cannot revoke a still-pending token. Some preparation logs also include tokens, increasing the audience that may see them even though owner binding remains required.
questions.Trade: Server-enforced supersession adds lifecycle bookkeeping and prevents stale confirmation. Keeping multiple live preparations is simpler but needs an honest user-visible model.
questions.Try: Prepare an amount, correct it, then try both tokens. Document current behavior and specify the desired supersession invariant.

questions.Q: Why must rate limiting, request-size limits, and tool budgets coexist?
questions.A: Request rate bounds arrival frequency, size limits bound per-request input, and tool or token budgets bound work initiated by one accepted request. An agent can turn one small request into many expensive provider calls, so requests per minute alone do not control cost.
questions.Why: Apply limits at request, run, model, and tool boundaries. Account for nested calls and retries so one accepted HTTP request cannot expand into unbounded downstream work.
questions.Risk: Fail-open Redis behavior preserves availability and can weaken fleet-wide limits during an outage. Model-generated loops may also stay within HTTP request limits while exhausting provider budgets.
questions.Trade: Layered budgets increase configuration and improve predictable resource use. Tight limits can interrupt legitimate multi-intent conversations and need explicit completion states.
questions.Try: Estimate worst-case cost from maximum turns, tool calls, retries, candidates, and output tokens. Test overload without using real private service requests.

questions.Q: How can error responses leak information even when access is denied?
questions.A: Different messages, status codes, timings, trace payloads, and raw exception strings can reveal record existence or internal details. A denial response should reveal only what the caller is entitled to learn, while internal diagnostics remain appropriately protected.
questions.Why: Return appropriately indistinguishable not-found or inaccessible responses when disclosure policy requires it. Keep private diagnostic detail in protected logs rather than client exception text.
questions.Risk: A model may repeat an internal error returned by a tool. Sanitizing only the final HTTP exception leaves tool results and streaming error events as additional channels.
questions.Trade: Generic external messages reduce detail for users and support; structured internal error categories preserve diagnosis without exposing private values.
questions.Try: Compare responses for unknown and foreign-owned request IDs, invalid tokens, provider failures, and database errors. Inspect both the streamed events and final response.

questions.Q: What does an effective threat-model review produce?
questions.A: It produces a concrete asset and actor map, trust boundaries, abuse cases, enforcement points, and tests. For this product, include private claim text, confirmation tokens, knowledge versions, prompt data, provider keys, session history, and traces.
questions.Why: List assets, actors, entry points, trust boundaries, and forbidden effects. Convert identified threats into owners, controls, and observable acceptance tests rather than a generic security checklist.
questions.Risk: A checklist detached from actual call sites can certify controls that are merely configured or documented. Threat modeling should include alternate paths such as evaluation, administration, scripts, and workers.
questions.Trade: A focused model tied to major workflows is maintainable. An exhaustive speculative catalog can consume time without improving concrete denial behavior.
questions.Try: Pick cross-user disclosure, duplicate submission, and malicious-source instructions. For each, identify the earliest reliable enforcement point and a test proving denial.

title: ADK agents, tools, and memory
subtitle: Understand the implemented runtime before comparing alternatives.

questions.Q: What makes this an agent rather than a fixed retrieval pipeline?
questions.A: A model can select tools, inspect results, and decide whether to continue before answering. A fixed pipeline executes a predetermined path for a known request shape. The example agent has bounded domain capabilities but flexible intent routing and multi-tool turns.
questions.Why: An agent chooses its next permitted action from observations; a fixed pipeline follows application-defined stages. Use model discretion only where it improves the task under measured constraints.
questions.Risk: Flexible selection introduces wrong-tool, repeated-tool, and premature-answer failures beyond retrieval quality. Tool availability should reflect server authorization, not only instructions saying which tools are appropriate.
questions.Trade: Agents handle conversational ambiguity and multiple intents while requiring trajectory evaluation and execution limits. A deterministic route remains preferable for exact confirmation and lifecycle mutation.
questions.Try: Compare a fixed policy-search endpoint with an ADK turn asking both a coverage and request-status question. Identify the additional decisions the agent makes.

questions.Q: How does the tool registry become a model-facing contract?
questions.A: The registry returns callable handlers. Their signatures and docstrings inform tool declarations; registry metadata and human descriptions are not automatically security enforcement or the exact text the model sees.
questions.Why: Define small tools with precise descriptions and typed inputs. Bind trusted identity outside model arguments and preserve business validation inside the service behind the tool.
questions.Risk: Adding requires_auth metadata does not prove authentication runs. Wrappers that alter signatures can also accidentally expose internal configuration or remove required field information.
questions.Trade: Function-derived tools are convenient and reduce duplicated schemas. They require disciplined annotations, docstrings, wrapper preservation, and server validation.
questions.Try: Inspect the generated declaration of prepare_request and compare it with a tool specification. Verify that owner identity is absent from model-controlled arguments.

questions.Q: Why preserve function signatures when instrumenting tools?
questions.A: Agent runtimes introspect callable signatures and annotations to construct schemas. A tracing wrapper can add internal parameters or change annotation resolution, causing the model to see a contract the underlying function does not support.
questions.Why: Instrumentation wrappers should preserve callable metadata used for schema generation. Verify the resulting advertised tool contract and avoid double wrapping or duplicate spans.
questions.Risk: A wrapper that preserves results but changes the model declaration can still break behavior. Likewise, exception-only success recording can classify a returned error payload as a successful call.
questions.Trade: Transparent instrumentation needs careful compatibility tests but keeps business tools vendor-neutral. Hand-instrumenting every function is simpler locally and prone to inconsistent coverage.
questions.Try: Compare inspect.signature and generated schema before and after instrumentation. Test both a raised exception and a returned success=False payload.

questions.Q: What does LiteLLM abstract, and what remains provider-specific?
questions.A: LiteLLM offers a common access surface for different model providers. Provider capabilities still vary in tool calling, structured output, token accounting, streaming, pricing, context windows, and error behavior. A common adapter does not make all models behaviorally interchangeable.
questions.Why: Treat the adapter as a compatibility layer rather than proof of identical provider behavior. Record the actual model and test tool use, structured output, cancellation, and usage reporting.
questions.Risk: A provider switch can change tool selection or output schemas without a Python type error. The example temperature override uses truthiness, so an explicit zero does not follow the same branch as a positive configured value.
questions.Trade: Routing flexibility reduces provider coupling while expanding the compatibility matrix. A single well-tested provider can be a sound early production choice.
questions.Try: Compare two providers on the same safe tool trajectories and output contracts. Test temperature zero separately from an omitted value.

questions.Q: How should agent memory be bounded and rehydrated?
questions.A: Retain enough recent user, assistant, and tool context to resolve references, while bounding replay and clearly separating temporary invocation state from persistent session state. Long history is not automatically useful context and may contain obsolete instructions or private data.
questions.Why: Select relevant recent history and validated working state under a budget. Rehydrate from authorized conversation records and retain durable operation identities across compaction.
questions.Risk: A lossy summary can forget corrected facts, retain an obsolete confirmation token, or misrepresent a previous tool failure. Message order and tool-result pairing need explicit tests.
questions.Trade: Compaction reduces tokens and latency while losing detail. Retrieving structured prior facts can be more reliable for critical values than trusting an unconstrained summary.
questions.Try: Create a conversation that corrects an amount, cancels a preparation, and returns later. Verify memory does not revive the old action.

questions.Q: Does a database-backed session service guarantee cross-replica continuity?
questions.A: It provides shared stored events and state when configured and healthy. Continuity also requires stable user/session resolution, compatible serialization, correct ordering, migration ownership, and a concurrency policy for overlapping turns. Durable storage alone does not serialize reasoning.
questions.Why: Choose a shared durable session store when cross-replica continuity is required. Test concurrent updates, message order, ownership, restart recovery, and migration rather than assuming persistence solves all continuity.
questions.Risk: Silent fallback can make one replica forget or diverge from another while health appears generally available. Runtime-created session tables also sit outside the ordinary Alembic ownership model.
questions.Trade: Fallback preserves some availability and weakens continuity. Production may need fail-closed readiness when shared conversation state is a required guarantee.
questions.Try: Start two replicas with explicit database sessions, then simulate storage initialization failure. Inspect the effective backend and continuity behavior.

questions.Q: Why distinguish a returned tool error from a raised exception?
questions.A: A tool can complete its Python call while returning found=False, success=False, or an error field. Those are domain outcomes, not necessarily exceptions. The agent, stream mapper, telemetry, and evaluation need a shared interpretation of those payloads.
questions.Why: Record transport success, function completion, and business outcome separately. A normal returned value can describe rejection or unavailability and must not become a successful task metric.
questions.Risk: Reporting every returned dictionary as success inflates reliability metrics. Treating every no-result as an error also misleads the user and can trigger unnecessary retries.
questions.Trade: Structured result types require more explicit schemas and simplify downstream interpretation. Free-form dictionaries are flexible and can accumulate incompatible conventions.
questions.Try: Define expected stream and metric outcomes for found=False, empty search, validation_errors, backend error, and a raised exception.

questions.Q: Why must a human handoff be more than a sentence in a prompt?
questions.A: A handoff needs an actual destination, case or ticket identity, permitted context transfer, status, and recovery if delivery fails. Saying that a specialist is being connected does not establish that any operational transfer occurred.
questions.Why: Create a real handoff record through a queue or case service. Report assignment state honestly and preserve a fallback when escalation infrastructure is unavailable.
questions.Risk: Users may believe a dispute or urgent request is being handled when the system only generated text. Evaluation should distinguish an escalation recommendation from a completed transfer.
questions.Trade: A real handoff integration adds external dependencies and privacy choices. An honest support-contact response is simpler and preferable to an unsupported promise.
questions.Try: Simulate a dispute and inspect all tool events. Specify a proposed escalation tool with success, pending, failed, and authorized-payload contracts.

questions.Q: How should agent execution be bounded?
questions.A: Bound model calls, tool calls, wall time, tokens, retries, and repeated identical actions. Use deterministic server checks for irreversible operations. A prompt asking the model not to repeat a tool is helpful guidance but not a hard execution ceiling.
questions.Why: Use a shared call, cost, and deadline budget for the whole task. Bound retries and repeated equivalent actions, and propagate cancellation through providers and tools.
questions.Risk: A looping agent can accumulate cost or keep a stream open while request-rate limits remain satisfied. A process-level cancellation may not stop already-started provider or worker operations.
questions.Trade: Tight limits improve predictability and can interrupt complex legitimate requests. Explicit partial-completion and escalation states preserve useful progress.
questions.Try: Use a fake model repeatedly requesting the same tool. Verify the host stops within a declared time and count budget and returns a truthful incomplete status.

questions.Q: How can deterministic tools and flexible reasoning coexist safely?
questions.A: Let the model interpret requests and propose a narrow operation; let deterministic validation, authorization, and transaction code decide whether and how that operation takes effect. The model's narrative should describe the authoritative result rather than manufacture it.
questions.Why: Keep flexible intent resolution outside deterministic authorization and transaction logic. The same narrow business service should enforce its rules regardless of the orchestration framework.
questions.Risk: A future tool that directly approves service requests or writes arbitrary status values would bypass the example authority model. Pattern consistency matters more than the orchestrator's brand.
questions.Trade: Narrow tools reduce open-ended autonomy but make actions auditable and testable. High-autonomy systems need equally strong capability and approval boundaries.
questions.Try: Design a proposed handler-assistance tool that recommends a decision without committing one. State who may approve it and which exact record becomes authoritative.

title: LangChain as an integration alternative
subtitle: Learn the abstractions while keeping business authority in existing services.

questions.Q: What would LangChain replace or add in this application?
questions.A: LangChain can supply model, message, tool, middleware, structured-output, and agent-building abstractions. Adopting its agent factory would replace part of the example ADK orchestration, not PostgreSQL, the retrieval service, domain validation, or the confirmation transaction.
questions.Why: Wrap existing services through compatible tool interfaces and retain business ownership and transactions. Compare the runtime with the baseline using identical application tasks and measured integration cost.
questions.Risk: Installing a framework without deciding who owns sessions, tool errors, and streaming can create two overlapping runtimes. A dependency change alone does not migrate behavioral contracts.
questions.Trade: LangChain offers a broad integration surface; staying with ADK avoids migration cost. Choose based on a demonstrated need and an equivalent behavioral benchmark.
questions.Try: Map each current ADK constructor argument to the proposed LangChain composition. Identify the contracts that should remain unchanged.

questions.Q: What are messages, chat models, and invocation methods?
