questions.A: Messages represent roles, text, tool calls, and tool results. A chat model consumes a message sequence and produces model output. Invocation, streaming, and batch methods are execution interfaces, not different authorization knowledge rules or independent guarantees of model quality.
questions.Why: Inject a compatible model interface and record provider-specific capabilities. A common constructor does not guarantee identical tool, streaming, or structured-output behavior.
questions.Risk: Dropping a tool result, role boundary, or corrected user value can change behavior. A model supporting text may not support the tool or structured-output features the application requires.
questions.Trade: Standard interfaces ease experimentation while provider capabilities still require testing. A single-provider direct adapter can be smaller for a narrow workload.
questions.Try: Translate a user question, tool call, tool result, and assistant answer into an explicit message sequence and verify the pairing identifiers.

questions.Q: How can an existing domain service become a LangChain tool?
questions.A: Wrap the existing async domain function with a narrow typed tool whose arguments contain only user-searchable input. Resolve trusted identity in server context and retain the domain function's validation and owner filters. The wrapper should not expose internal session or owner parameters to the model.
questions.Why: Expose a narrow model-facing function that calls an authorized service with trusted runtime context. Keep internal owner and tenant arguments out of user-editable tool schemas.
questions.Risk: A convenient wrapper accepting user_id from the model defeats the example scoping boundary. Context setup and reset must be defined for HTTP, evaluation, and background execution.
questions.Trade: Thin adapters reuse tested business logic and add a small compatibility surface. Rewriting tools inside each framework risks policy drift.
questions.Try: Inspect the proposed read-only policy wrapper in the worked examples. Add a service requests wrapper that obtains identity from a trusted service context.

questions.Q: How do runnable composition and an agent loop differ?
questions.A: A composed chain follows a known sequence such as retrieve, assemble, and answer. An agent loop lets a model choose tools and continuation. Both can use the same model and retriever interfaces, but they create different testing and cost requirements.
questions.Why: Use fixed composition when stage order is known; use an agent loop when tool selection depends on observations. Evaluate the extra flexibility against latency and failure complexity.
questions.Risk: Calling a fixed chain an agent can hide the absence of planning; calling an agent a simple chain can hide repeated calls and nondeterministic routing. Name the actual control flow.
questions.Trade: Fixed composition is easier to bound and diagnose; flexible routing handles ambiguity. Start from the least flexible flow that meets the requirement.
questions.Try: Build a deterministic retrieval-and-answer baseline and compare it with agent orchestration on single-intent and multi-intent cases.

questions.Q: What does structured output validate, and what does it not validate?
questions.A: A structured schema constrains the form and types of a model result, such as an answer with citation IDs and a status. It does not prove the citations exist, the amounts match policy text, or the caller may execute a proposed action.
questions.Why: Choose a compatible structured-output strategy, parse the result, and run domain validation. Schema compliance does not establish factual correctness or action authority.
questions.Risk: A valid JSON decision saying approved is still not an authorized claim transition. Schema conformance can otherwise create a false impression of factual or business correctness.
questions.Trade: Typed outputs simplify UI integration and require explicit parse, retry, and semantic-validation branches. Free-form prose is flexible and harder to validate reliably.
questions.Try: Define a recommendation schema with status, cited evidence IDs, missing facts, and explanation. Reject unknown citations before presentation.

questions.Q: What belongs in middleware instead of a business tool?
questions.A: Cross-cutting knowledge rules such as call budgets, model selection, standardized error mapping, and context preparation can sit around execution. Business tools should still own their domain authorization, validation, and transaction behavior.
questions.Why: Use middleware for cross-cutting policy, budget, logging, and context transformations. Keep business validation in application services so non-agent callers enforce the same invariants.
questions.Risk: A middleware-only authorization check can be bypassed by direct service calls. Overly broad retry middleware can also repeat side effects whose business idempotency is not established.
questions.Trade: Central hooks reduce repetition while increasing execution-order and wrapper-compatibility complexity. Keep critical invariants enforceable independently of orchestration hooks.
questions.Try: Classify budget checking, owner filtering, signature preservation, and pending-token consumption by the layer that must enforce each one.

questions.Q: How should short-term memory map to support conversations?
questions.A: Short-term memory stores a thread's evolving conversational context. It needs a stable thread identity and a persistence policy. Long-term customer facts, authoritative service requests, and pending confirmation state should remain in domain storage rather than only in a message buffer.
questions.Why: Map conversation and thread ownership explicitly, define retention and compaction, and test concurrent updates. Framework memory is neither a business ledger nor a universal persistence contract.
questions.Risk: Reusing thread IDs across users or forgetting ownership checks can disclose history. Memory summaries can also retain obsolete tokens or knowledge facts after a correction.
questions.Trade: Persistent memory improves continuity and increases retention obligations. Stateless turns simplify privacy and require more explicit context from the user.
questions.Try: Design a user-and-conversation thread key and a migration test for archived history, corrected facts, and sign-out followed by another user.

questions.Q: How should LangChain streams be adapted to the existing UI contract?
questions.A: Translate framework-specific chunks into the application's typed events rather than exposing raw runtime objects. Preserve text deltas, tool activity, errors, persisted message IDs, and a truthful terminal status.
questions.Why: Translate framework events into a stable user-safe schema. Preserve task identity, event order, cancellation, errors, and persistence-before-completion semantics across adapters.
questions.Risk: A tool error or cancelled stream can otherwise be mislabeled complete. Forwarding arbitrary runtime state may leak internal or private fields.
questions.Trade: A stable application event layer costs adapter code and decouples UI releases from framework changes. Raw framework streams are faster to demo and fragile to evolve.
questions.Try: Feed equivalent synthetic ADK and LangChain event sequences into two adapters and compare the resulting public events.

questions.Q: Are framework guardrails a replacement for deterministic permissions?
questions.A: No. Guardrails can classify inputs, validate outputs, or interrupt unsafe model behavior, but backend authorization must still deny prohibited reads and writes. A classifier can be wrong or unavailable, and a prompt can be ignored.
questions.Why: Validate both proposed arguments and actual service outcomes. A tool description improves selection but cannot prevent a model from proposing unauthorized or invalid operations.
questions.Risk: A content-safety pass does not certify that a customer may access another claim or approve a payout. Combining unrelated notions of safety into one boolean hides authority errors.
questions.Trade: Guardrails add useful signals and latency. Deploy them as complementary checks with explicit error behavior, not as the sole permission system.
questions.Try: Make a simulated model issue an unauthorized operation after a guardrail reports safe text. Verify the service still denies it.

questions.Q: How would you decide whether a runtime-to-LangChain migration is worthwhile?
questions.A: Compare required integrations, operational complexity, framework support, team familiarity, migration risk, and measured behavior. Require parity on tool routing, scope enforcement, confirmation, streaming, memory, evaluation, and tracing before changing the production runtime.
questions.Why: Compare routing, scope enforcement, approval, memory, streaming, recovery, and trace privacy on the same fixtures. Preserve product contracts or explicitly redesign them with migration and rollback evidence.
questions.Risk: Benchmarking only a successful coverage response misses multi-turn correction, tool failure, and duplicate writes. New abstractions can also change trace payload disclosure.
questions.Trade: A better-fit ecosystem can justify the cost; keeping the example stack may be more valuable when problems are domain contracts rather than orchestration limitations.
questions.Try: Write an architecture decision record with one concrete unmet need, a parity checklist, a limited experiment, and a rollback condition.

title: LangGraph stateful workflows
subtitle: Design an explicit workflow without confusing checkpoints with business commits.

questions.Q: What problem would LangGraph solve that a basic agent loop does not?
questions.A: LangGraph expresses a workflow as state, nodes, and transitions, with explicit branching and persistence options. It is useful when retries, human review, resumability, and bounded stages should be visible in the orchestration design rather than left entirely to a model loop.
questions.Why: Represent explicit state transitions when the workflow needs branching, checkpoints, review, or recovery. Keep a simple agent loop when those requirements do not justify a graph.
questions.Risk: A graph diagram can suggest stronger guarantees than its nodes implement. Domain writes still need their own transaction and permission boundaries.
questions.Trade: Explicit control improves inspectability while adding state schema and orchestration code. A simple tool-calling loop can remain sufficient for narrow conversational tasks.
questions.Try: Draw a proposed eligibility-review graph with answerable, missing-facts, unavailable-backend, and escalation branches before writing nodes.

questions.Q: How do StateGraph state, nodes, and conditional edges work together?
questions.A: State is the workflow's shared data contract; nodes compute updates; edges choose what executes next. A node can be deterministic code or a model call. Conditional routing should use validated state rather than treating arbitrary generated text as an unrestricted next-node name.
questions.Why: Define typed state with clear ownership, transient fields, durable references, and terminal outcomes. Store large artifacts separately and keep versioned IDs inside graph state.
questions.Risk: Overloaded state can retain private text, credentials, or stale authorization. Input schema shape alone does not decide what a stream or trace may disclose.
questions.Trade: Explicit state improves testing and requires careful versioning. A dictionary with unrestricted keys is flexible and harder to migrate or secure.
questions.Try: Separate public output fields, internal evidence references, and trusted identity in the proposed graph contract.

questions.Q: Why do reducers matter when graph nodes run in parallel?
questions.A: A reducer defines how multiple updates to a state field combine. Replacing a value, appending messages, and merging keyed results are different semantics. Parallel branches need a declared merge rule rather than assuming the last writer is correct.
questions.Why: Give parallel updates explicit merge semantics through compatible reducers. Decide whether lists append, records replace, or conflicts fail; persistence alone does not define a safe merge.
questions.Risk: An append reducer can duplicate retries, and a merge can combine evidence from incompatible revisions or scopes. A reducer is not a distributed database transaction.
questions.Trade: Explicit merge rules support parallel work and require identity, ordering, and replay discipline. Sequential nodes avoid some conflicts at the cost of latency.
questions.Try: Design a reducer for evidence keyed by source, revision, and chunk ID. Show how repeated delivery avoids duplicating the same item.

questions.Q: What is a checkpoint, and how is it different from a business commit?
questions.A: A checkpoint stores workflow state so execution can resume or be inspected. A business commit makes an authoritative business transition durable. A checkpoint can refer to a completed operation, but saving it does not atomically commit another service's database transaction.
questions.Why: Treat checkpoints as workflow progress records. Reconcile them with authoritative operation status after crashes, because checkpoint persistence and a separate business transaction may not commit together.
questions.Risk: On resume, a node may retry an already-completed side effect. An in-memory saver demonstrates state handling only within its lifetime and is not a durable production guarantee.
questions.Trade: Durable checkpoints support recovery and require storage, retention, access policy, and schema evolution. Pure in-memory graphs are easier for local experiments.
questions.Try: Draw a crash after business commit but before checkpoint save. Specify how an operation ID lets the resumed node discover the existing result.

questions.Q: How does a human-review interrupt differ from authorization?
questions.A: An interrupt pauses workflow progress and exposes a question or proposed action for review. Authorization determines whether the identity resuming it is permitted to approve that exact action. A resume payload saying approved is untrusted unless the server validates its actor and scope.
questions.Why: Pause execution for input or review, then validate the resumed principal and approval against current business state. A resume command is control flow, not authorization.
questions.Risk: Guessable or cross-user thread access can resume another person's workflow. Material edits after review can invalidate what was approved even if the resume token is technically valid.
questions.Trade: Human pauses reduce accidental actions while adding persistence and expiry management. For low-risk reads they may be unnecessary.
questions.Try: Bind a proposed review to user, payload hash, operation ID, and expiry. Test an unauthorized resume and a changed amount.

questions.Q: Why must code before an interrupt or retry be safe to execute again?
questions.A: Resuming or recovering a workflow may re-enter node code. Work performed before the pause can therefore repeat. Deterministic computation is usually safe; sending a notification or creating a service request needs a durable idempotent operation boundary.
questions.Why: Put nondeterministic and side-effecting work behind replay-safe boundaries. Use durable operation keys and test the crash window after an effect but before checkpoint completion.
questions.Risk: Repeating a preparation can leave multiple live tokens; repeating an external notification can confuse the user. A cached Python return value is not enough across process crashes.
questions.Trade: Smaller nodes with explicit side-effect tasks improve replay reasoning and add orchestration detail. One large node is shorter and harder to recover safely.
questions.Try: Put a harmless counter and a mock external action before a teaching interrupt. Observe replay, then move the action behind an idempotent service contract.

questions.Q: How should graph retries and timeouts be layered?
questions.A: Retry only failures likely to recover, with bounded attempts and an overall deadline. A node retry, provider retry, database retry, and client retry can multiply each other. Track the full operation budget and avoid retrying invalid authorization or schema errors.
questions.Why: Layer node retries, provider retries, and task deadlines deliberately. Count all attempts in one budget and classify business rejection separately from transient infrastructure failure.
questions.Risk: Nested retries amplify load and can execute write nodes repeatedly. A model timeout also does not prove the provider or remote agent stopped processing.
questions.Trade: Local resilience helps transient failures, while a simpler centralized budget is easier to reason about. Use stage-specific policy with one overall ceiling.
questions.Try: Calculate worst-case attempts for two client retries, three node attempts, and four provider attempts. Replace that accidental multiplier with an explicit budget.

questions.Q: Can graph private state be streamed safely by default?
questions.A: Do not assume a private schema is a redaction policy. A framework may stream internal state or custom events depending on mode. Define an application event projection that allowlists public fields and removes private evidence, identity, and credentials.
questions.Why: Project only approved fields into public events. State needed for internal coordination can include private evidence, tool arguments, or identifiers that should not be streamed.
questions.Risk: Forwarding raw values or updates can expose claim details or internal analysis. A UI that hides a field visually has still received it over the network.
questions.Trade: Allowlisted projections take adapter work and preserve privacy across framework updates. Raw graph streaming is convenient for development diagnostics only under controlled access.
questions.Try: Insert a synthetic private field into graph state and inspect every chosen stream mode. Verify the public SSE adapter never emits it.

questions.Q: How should graph state and checkpoints evolve across deployments?
questions.A: Version state schemas and maintain readers or migrations for active checkpoints. A suspended service workflow may resume after code changes, so renamed fields, changed node semantics, and new authorization requirements need compatibility handling.
questions.Why: Version checkpoint schemas and migrate or isolate old threads deliberately. Test resume with old artifacts after deployment, and prevent incompatible readers from silently interpreting changed state fields.
questions.Risk: A resumed old workflow can invoke a new write path with stale assumptions. Authorization should be re-evaluated at action time rather than frozen indefinitely in a checkpoint.
questions.Trade: Compatibility readers increase maintenance and preserve resumability. Expiring old workflows simplifies migration but must communicate how users restart safely.
questions.Try: Design a v1-to-v2 checkpoint migration that adds rule revision and payload hash before confirmation. Specify what happens if the old evidence no longer exists.

questions.Q: When is LangGraph a better choice than ADK or a plain function?
questions.A: Choose it when explicit state transitions, branching, durable pause/resume, or inspectable parallel work solve a real product requirement. Keep a plain function for deterministic small operations and consider retaining ADK when flexible tool routing already meets the need.
questions.Why: Evaluate transitions, terminal outcomes, approvals, replay, and cost under realistic failures. A passing graph visualization or one happy-path invocation does not establish business reliability.
questions.Risk: Introducing a graph solely to draw a more impressive architecture can add persistence and deployment obligations without improving outcomes. More orchestration layers can also fragment traces and ownership.
questions.Trade: Explicit workflow control is valuable when recovery and review dominate. Simpler code is preferable when the path is short and has no durable pauses.
questions.Try: Write a decision record for one proposed graph workflow and one operation you deliberately keep as a normal function. Defend both choices.

title: A2A and distributed agent collaboration
subtitle: Treat remote agents as services with identity, tasks, and failure—not shared thoughts.

questions.Q: What is A2A, and when should a backend expose a remote agent?
questions.A: Agent2Agent describes interaction between independently hosted agents, including discovery, messages, tasks, and outputs. Use it when a remote specialist has a genuine service boundary rather than wrapping an ordinary deterministic lookup in another agent.
questions.Why: A remote agent integration needs explicit client and server adapters, discovery, identity, task state, and a sharing policy. An agent SDK dependency does not create an operational endpoint.
questions.Risk: Calling two local functions agents is not proof of protocol interoperability. A diagram arrow labeled A2A must correspond to an implemented and version-tested transport contract.
questions.Trade: A2A can support organizational and runtime boundaries while adding network, identity, compatibility, and operational complexity. A local domain service is simpler when independent deployment is unnecessary.
questions.Try: Identify one support capability that genuinely needs an independently operated agent and one that should remain an ordinary local tool.

questions.Q: How do A2A, MCP, and ordinary APIs differ?
questions.A: A2A concerns agent-to-agent interactions and task-oriented collaboration. MCP commonly exposes tools and resources to model-enabled clients. A normal API can provide deterministic domain operations without claiming to be an autonomous peer. These interfaces can coexist but do not grant authority by themselves.
questions.Why: Use MCP for AI-facing capability access, ordinary APIs for deterministic service operations, and A2A where remote agent task ownership is useful. Define who owns every durable effect.
questions.Risk: Treating a peer agent as a trusted internal function can bypass user scope or disclose entire conversations. Capability discovery is not consent to every requested action.
questions.Trade: Protocol choice affects interoperability and lifecycle semantics. Use the narrowest interface that meets the integration need rather than wrapping every endpoint in an agent protocol.
questions.Try: Map policy search, request confirmation, long-running specialist review, and metrics export to appropriate interfaces and explain the decision.

questions.Q: What is an Agent Card, and why is it not an authorization token?
questions.A: An Agent Card describes an agent's identity, capabilities, skills, endpoint, and security requirements. Discovery helps a client select a compatible service. Credentials and authorization are separately validated when invoking protected operations.
questions.Why: Treat published capability metadata as untrusted service input. Review the endpoint and supported contracts before sending scoped customer context or delegating a task.
questions.Risk: A malicious or stale card can point at an unintended endpoint or overstate capabilities. Do not send credentials or private claim data to arbitrary discovered destinations without trust and network policy.
questions.Trade: Dynamic discovery improves flexibility and adds authenticity, caching, and allowlist requirements. Explicitly configured peers are simpler for a small controlled deployment.
questions.Try: Draft a secret-free capability description for a review-only specialist. List information that belongs in deployment configuration rather than its public card.

questions.Q: How do messages, tasks, and artifacts differ in A2A?
questions.A: A message is an exchange of content, a task represents tracked work with lifecycle state, and an artifact is an output produced by that work. A reply being delivered does not necessarily mean the task completed or its output is authorized for all users.
questions.Why: Map remote lifecycle states into a versioned internal task model. Preserve remote identifiers, required user input, cancellation state, and authoritative completion references.
questions.Risk: Treating progress text as a final approved decision can trigger premature downstream action. Artifact references also need ownership, integrity, revision, and retrieval limits.
questions.Trade: Explicit tasks support long-running work and require durable tracking. One synchronous response is easier when the operation is genuinely short.
questions.Try: Design an internal task record for a review request with owner, remote ID, status, result reference, deadline, and idempotency key.

questions.Q: How should remote-agent authentication and user delegation work?
questions.A: Authenticate the service peer and separately authorize the delegated action for the originating user or case. A service identity should receive only the evidence and actions needed for its task. Do not forward a browser cookie indiscriminately across organizational boundaries.
questions.Why: Authenticate the remote service and delegate only the minimum user authority required. Verify token audience and avoid sending a broad application credential as a convenience.
questions.Risk: A powerful remote agent can become a confused deputy, using its own privileges for a caller who lacks them. Agent-card metadata does not enforce resource authorization.
questions.Trade: Narrow delegated capabilities reduce disclosure and require identity integration. Broad shared credentials simplify demos and make accountability difficult.
questions.Try: Define which identity approves a review, which identity reads evidence, and which identity may confirm a service request. Keep final write authority local unless explicitly delegated.

questions.Q: How do remote retries avoid duplicate work?
questions.A: Give one logical request a stable operation identity, persist its relationship to the remote task, and query or reconcile before creating another task after an ambiguous timeout. Transport request IDs and business idempotency keys may serve different purposes.
questions.Why: Propagate deadlines and durable operation identity across retries. After an uncertain response, query task status rather than automatically restarting a side-effecting remote task.
questions.Risk: A timeout can mean the remote service accepted the task but the acknowledgment was lost. Blind retries can create duplicate cases, charges, or conflicting recommendations.
questions.Trade: Reconciliation adds storage and latency but avoids assuming failure from missing acknowledgment. Fire-and-forget messaging is smaller and unsuitable for untracked consequential work.
questions.Try: Simulate remote acceptance followed by a dropped response. Show how the client discovers or reuses the original task without submitting twice.

questions.Q: What does cancellation mean for a remote agent task?
questions.A: Cancellation is a request to stop eligible work, not proof that every side effect has been undone. A task may have completed or crossed an irreversible boundary before the cancellation arrives. The host must interpret the remote result and reconcile its own state.
questions.Why: Specify what cancellation can stop and what already completed. A remote cancelled state does not reverse an external effect, so expose authoritative status and compensation where appropriate.
questions.Risk: Closing the browser stream does not establish task cancellation. A user may otherwise believe a case was abandoned while remote work continues or a notification is delivered.
questions.Trade: Explicit cancellation acknowledgment improves user expectations and adds race handling. Letting tasks finish is operationally simpler for read-only work if clearly communicated.
questions.Try: Draw cancellation before acceptance, during review, and after completion. Define the displayed state and permissible follow-up action for each race.

questions.Q: How can A2A artifacts become a prompt-injection or disclosure channel?
questions.A: A remote result can contain untrusted text, URLs, attachments, or instructions. Treat it as data from a service with a specific trust level, validate its schema, and allowlist any subsequent action. Remote output must not inherit system-instruction authority.
questions.Why: Constrain outputs by schema, scope, size, provenance, and retention. Validate artifacts before using them as facts or displaying them through a privileged renderer.
questions.Risk: An artifact can ask the model to retrieve another customer's claim or fetch an internal URL. Authentication of the sender does not make every returned instruction safe or every referenced document authorized.
questions.Trade: Rich artifacts support useful collaboration and need validation, size limits, safe fetching, and provenance. Minimal structured references are easier to govern than entire conversations and attachments.
questions.Try: Return a mock artifact containing a cross-tenant reference and an instruction to bypass confirmation. Verify neither is executed.

questions.Q: How should one trace span cross an A2A boundary?
questions.A: Propagate an approved trace context and stable operation identifiers while keeping credentials and private content separate. Each service records its own spans and outcome; the host correlates the remote task with the originating operation.
questions.Why: Pass safe trace context under a reviewed policy and retain task correlation across services. Distributed spans aid diagnosis but do not establish who authorized an operation.
questions.Risk: A trace ID is not authentication, and untrusted inbound trace metadata needs validation. Copying full claim text into span attributes can leak it to both organizations' telemetry systems.
questions.Trade: Distributed traces speed diagnosis but require shared conventions and retention policy. Correlation by sanitized operation IDs is a simpler fallback.
questions.Try: Design a trace tree for one remote review with a retry and later artifact delivery. Show which spans represent waiting versus remote execution.

questions.Q: When is a multi-agent architecture justified for service work?
questions.A: Use independently scoped agents when capabilities have distinct ownership, data access, deployment, or specialist review responsibilities. A local planner calling five functions does not need networked peers simply to look sophisticated.
questions.Why: Use multiple agents when ownership, capabilities, trust, or deployment boundaries justify them. Compare with one local agent and deterministic services before accepting the coordination overhead.
questions.Risk: More peers increase routing errors, coordination cost, inconsistent evidence, and cascading failures. Agreement between agents is not independent verification if they share the same wrong source or model.
questions.Trade: Specialization and organizational boundaries can justify distributed collaboration; a single orchestrator with narrow tools is cheaper and easier to test.
questions.Try: Write an A2A architecture decision record with a task lifecycle, delegation policy, data-minimization plan, failure budget, and a simpler alternative.

title: Evaluating agents and application outcomes
subtitle: Measure the trajectory and durable effects, not just a fluent answer.

questions.Q: Why is answer evaluation insufficient for an agent?
questions.A: An answer can sound correct after using the wrong tool, revealing unauthorized information, repeating an expensive action, or failing to commit the intended operation. Agent evaluation needs task success, tool choice and arguments, permissions, side effects, recovery, and final communication.
questions.Why: Define task outcomes and forbidden effects before choosing metrics. Evaluate tools and durable state as well as final text, then use traces to identify the failing layer.
questions.Risk: A model judge can reward a statement that a service request was submitted even when no claim exists. Conversely, a safely rejected operation may sound less helpful while being the correct outcome.
questions.Trade: Multi-layer evaluation needs more fixtures and gives actionable diagnosis. One aggregate answer score is easier to display and weaker as a release gate.
questions.Try: Create three cases with identical final text but different underlying tool and database histories. Define which pass and why.

questions.Q: How do reference trajectories and invariant-based trajectories differ?
questions.A: A reference trajectory compares observed calls with an expected sequence. An invariant checks necessary properties such as owner scoping, no duplicate confirmation, and policy retrieval before an eligibility determination. Different valid tool sequences may satisfy the same task.
questions.Why: Use exact reference sequences only for required order. Prefer invariants or partial orders when several legitimate trajectories can complete the task without violating scope or approval.
questions.Risk: Exact sequence tests can fail harmless reordering; very loose rubrics can miss a missing critical step. Tool names alone also ignore whether arguments or results were correct.
questions.Trade: Reference paths are easy to inspect and brittle under valid variation. Invariants need careful definition and better express safety and business requirements.
questions.Try: Evaluate a mixed coverage/status request with two valid call orders, then reject both if the service request lookup lacks the correct owner context.

questions.Q: What do retrieval-only, context, and end-to-end evaluations measure?
questions.A: Retrieval-only evaluation measures candidate quality. Context evaluation examines the evidence assembled for generation. End-to-end evaluation checks the actual answer, agent actions, and relevant durable outcome. Each localizes a different failure class.
questions.Why: Record whether an output came from retrieval, context assembly, a baseline, or the live agent. Compare the same path across releases and label synthetic substitutes explicitly.
questions.Risk: Comparing proxy scores with live-agent scores without checking labels can create a false regression or improvement. Availability fallbacks should never silently change the meaning of the reported metric.
questions.Trade: Offline proxies are cheap and useful for early diagnosis. Actual agent evaluation costs provider calls and measures a different layer.
questions.Try: Run or inspect configurations for all modes and assert the reported answer_source. Separate proxy and live results in your report.

questions.Q: How should a multi-turn request-preparation test be structured?
questions.A: Model the user's progressive facts, corrections, missing fields, preparation, and explicit confirmation boundary. Assert the prepared payload and server effects at each step, not only whether the assistant eventually produces a token.
questions.Why: Create multi-turn fixtures with missing fields, corrections, stale approvals, cancellation, and repeated submission. Assert both the user interaction and the final business state.
questions.Risk: A user simulator may accidentally supply hints or accept a fabricated success. Test fixtures should inspect the database and use deterministic assertions for required fields and token state.
questions.Trade: Multi-turn tests take more execution and reveal memory and correction failures absent from isolated prompts. Keep a small high-value regression set alongside larger sampled evaluations.
questions.Try: Create a scenario that changes the amount after preparation and attempts the old token. Report both current behavior and the desired contract.

questions.Q: How should refusal and clarification be evaluated separately?
questions.A: Refusal is appropriate when the task is unsupported or evidence cannot justify an answer. Clarification is appropriate when obtaining missing facts could make the task answerable. Escalation is another outcome requiring truthful operational status.
questions.Why: Distinguish unavailable evidence, unsupported intent, missing user information, and denied authority. Evaluate whether the response chooses the correct refusal, clarification, or retry behavior.
questions.Risk: Rewarding all refusals as safe can produce an unusable assistant. Rewarding direct answers to ambiguous eligibility questions can produce unsupported decisions.
questions.Trade: Rich outcome labels cost annotation effort and better match product expectations. A binary correct/incorrect label is simpler and loses diagnostic detail.
questions.Try: Label cases as answer, clarify, refuse, retry, or escalate. Require evidence for every final coverage claim and an actual handoff result before claiming transfer.

questions.Q: How can evaluation verify that writes happened exactly as intended?
questions.A: Assert durable rows, ownership, consumed-token state, lifecycle events, and outbox records after the operation. Repeat and race requests to verify logical uniqueness. Evaluate external deliveries separately from database acceptance.
questions.Why: Run against disposable services with an effect ledger. Count writes, approvals, owners, and operation keys; a convincing success message cannot replace database assertions.
questions.Risk: A mocked submit function can return success without exercising SQL locks or commits. A judge of answer text cannot establish atomicity or idempotency.
questions.Trade: Real integration tests are slower and necessary for authoritative effects. Cheap fake-model tests remain useful for routing and error mapping around them.
questions.Try: Build a failure-injection table for every write in confirmation. For each failure, assert the visible claim, submission, event, and job state.

questions.Q: How should a judge be calibrated and protected from the answer being judged?
questions.A: Use a precise rubric, trusted references, known positive and negative cases, and human review to measure agreement. Treat candidate answer and retrieved text as untrusted data in the judge prompt. Record judge model, prompt, and sampling settings.
questions.Why: Calibrate judges against human-reviewed labels, keep answer text untrusted, and version the rubric and model. Track disagreements and test adversarial scoring instructions.
questions.Risk: A candidate can contain instructions to the judge, and a judge can favor style over factual support. A second model is not independent truth when it shares the same missing evidence.
questions.Trade: Model judging scales nuanced review and costs money and uncertainty. Deterministic checks should handle exact citations, amounts, permissions, and state transitions where possible.
questions.Try: Add a fluent unsupported answer and a judge-injection answer to a calibration set. Compare model verdicts with explicit human labels.

questions.Q: How do uncertainty intervals and category slices improve evaluation?
questions.A: A score from a small sample is an estimate, not a universal property. Report sample counts, uncertainty, and important categories such as exclusions, limits, corrections, unanswerable questions, and authorization failures. Inspect severity as well as frequency.
questions.Why: Report sample counts, confidence or uncertainty intervals, and meaningful task slices. Avoid claiming a small aggregate score proves equivalent quality across languages or difficult cases.
questions.Risk: Repeatedly tuning on the same visible cases overfits the benchmark. Averaging a cross-user disclosure with several harmless formatting errors gives a misleading quality summary.
questions.Trade: Category reporting creates more numbers and reveals actionable regressions. Small categories need cautious interpretation rather than overconfident ranking.
questions.Try: Split a benchmark by answerability and category, publish counts, and flag critical failures as release blockers instead of averaging them away.

questions.Q: How should evaluation control cost and side effects?
questions.A: Separate deterministic unit tests, offline retrieval checks, fake-model trajectories, and opt-in live-agent runs. Use synthetic identities and a sandbox, forbid real irreversible actions, and bound tokens, calls, and total spend. Record which execution mode actually ran.
questions.Why: Use synthetic identities, isolated data, and sandbox endpoints. Bound judge calls and agent retries, and never let an evaluation trigger real payments or customer notifications.
questions.Risk: A live agent can prepare records or call real services if its test capabilities are not constrained. Test traces may also export fixtures containing private data.
questions.Trade: Offline checks are fast and less realistic; live runs expose provider behavior and require stronger controls. Use both without conflating their scores.
questions.Try: Define a CI budget and a nightly live-evaluation budget with safe tool replacements and explicit answer-source assertions.

questions.Q: What should an agent release gate require?
questions.A: Require critical authorization and write invariants, non-regression on held-out task outcomes, acceptable latency and cost, and a rollback path. Keep quality thresholds distinct from informational efficiency metrics. A release gate should reflect product harm and operational capacity.
questions.Why: Predeclare release gates for critical invariants, task quality, latency, and cost. Keep immutable run manifests, reviewed failures, and a rollback artifact for the selected release.
questions.Risk: A changing judge or proxy fallback can move metrics without a real behavior change. A passing average must never excuse a critical cross-user disclosure or duplicate write.
questions.Trade: Strict gates slow some releases and prevent expensive regressions. Narrow deterministic checks should fail quickly before costly live evaluation.
questions.Try: Write a gate with hard denials, category quality thresholds, p95 latency, cost per successful task, and explicit metadata compatibility checks.

title: Agent and RAG evaluation libraries
subtitle: Choose tools by measurement need, data access, and reproducibility.

questions.Q: How do you choose an evaluation library without turning the stack into a collection of dashboards?
questions.A: Start from the question to measure: retrieval relevance, grounded answers, tool trajectories, task completion, adversarial behavior, or production drift. Choose one durable experiment record and connect additional metrics only where they add diagnostic value.
questions.Why: Choose tools by the question they can measure, required input data, workflow fit, privacy, and cost. A growing collection of dashboards is not an evaluation strategy.
questions.Risk: Different tools may use the same metric name for different inputs, judges, and aggregation rules. Comparing their numeric outputs without recording definitions is invalid.
questions.Trade: One harness is easier to operate; specialized libraries can deepen particular checks. Prefer a small adapter around a shared dataset and result schema.
questions.Try: Create a selection matrix for ADK evaluation, LangSmith, Ragas, DeepEval, TruLens, Phoenix, and Promptfoo. State one justified use and one limitation for each.

questions.Q: What does ADK evaluation add for this example ADK agent?
questions.A: ADK evaluation can test tool-use trajectories and final responses using reference or rubric-based criteria. Its fit is strongest when you want evaluation close to the runtime's sessions and events, including reviewed multi-turn cases.
questions.Why: Use compatible ADK evaluation interfaces for agent-specific criteria where they fit the runtime. Verify which criteria actually ran and retain application-level transaction and authorization tests separately.
questions.Risk: Exact trajectory matching can reject valid alternative orders, and judge-based criteria add model dependencies and cost. Some criteria require additional services; the dependency's broad lower bound does not guarantee every current documentation feature exists locally.
questions.Trade: Runtime-native evaluation reduces event translation and may couple fixtures to the framework. A framework-neutral contract suite survives migration more easily.
questions.Try: Define one exact confirmation-preparation trajectory and one rubric for flexible coverage review. Pin versions before running the documented criterion configuration.

questions.Q: What is LangSmith evaluation useful for if the agent uses ADK?
questions.A: LangSmith supports datasets, experiments, evaluators, and review workflows that need not require LangChain as the agent runtime. The application can submit its own target function and measured outputs while retaining ADK execution.
questions.Why: Use dataset, experiment, and trace workflows independently of a particular orchestrator where supported. Integrate through a narrow adapter and review what payloads leave the application.
questions.Risk: Uploading examples, outputs, or traces can disclose claim data. Experiment identity must distinguish model output from an offline context proxy and preserve prompt, corpus, and evaluator revisions.
questions.Trade: A shared experiment service improves collaboration and adds data-governance and service-dependency considerations. Local JSON reports are easier to keep isolated and less convenient for team review.
questions.Try: Design a target function returning answer, evidence IDs, tool trace, and answer_source for one synthetic case. Specify which fields may be exported.

questions.Q: How does Ragas help evaluate retrieval-augmented answers?
questions.A: Ragas provides metrics for relationships among questions, retrieved contexts, answers, and references. Faithfulness asks whether answer service requests are supported by context; other metrics address relevance and retrieval behavior. Each metric has required inputs and may use a model judge.
questions.Why: Match each Ragas metric to its required context, answer, reference, and judge inputs. Pin the implementation and do not assume every metric is reference-free or comparable across versions.
questions.Risk: Faithfulness to the wrong rule revision can still score well. Missing references, synthetic contexts, and judge changes can alter meaning or cost.
questions.Trade: Specialized RAG diagnostics help isolate failure layers and do not establish authorization, exact-money calculations, or correct claim writes. Keep those deterministic tests separate.
questions.Try: Compare an answer faithful to stale evidence with an answer correct for the active policy. Explain why both evidence applicability and faithfulness must be evaluated.

questions.Q: How does DeepEval fit into a pytest-oriented workflow?
questions.A: DeepEval provides test-case and metric abstractions for language-model systems, including faithfulness evaluation over retrieval context. It can make selected behavioral quality checks part of an existing test workflow while still depending on judge configuration for relevant metrics.
questions.Why: Represent a task with the required test-case fields and choose a DeepEval metric suited to the rubric. Record judge configuration and retain deterministic business-invariant checks alongside it.
questions.Risk: A unit-test appearance can conceal network calls, nondeterminism, and cost. A passing metric does not prove server-side authorization or transaction atomicity.
questions.Trade: Developer-friendly tests improve feedback locality; broad judge-heavy CI can become slow and flaky. Run exact contract tests frequently and sampled model judging under a controlled budget.
questions.Try: Add one faithful and one unsupported answer to an optional evaluation suite, pin the judge configuration, and record raw verdicts alongside thresholds.

questions.Q: What does the TruLens RAG triad measure?
questions.A: The RAG triad distinguishes context relevance, groundedness of the response in context, and answer relevance to the question. Separating these relationships helps identify whether retrieval or generation deserves investigation.
questions.Why: Treat context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance as distinct questions. Define feedback inputs and calibrate scores before using any RAG triad as a release decision.
questions.Risk: Good triad scores do not establish that the policy applies to this user or that a submitted claim exists. Domain and permission checks remain outside those semantic relationships.
questions.Trade: Structured feedback improves diagnosis while adding instrumentation and evaluator configuration. Use it when the team will act on the distinctions rather than only collect more scores.
questions.Try: Create three failures: irrelevant context, unsupported answer, and grounded but off-topic answer. Map each to the relationship that should fail.

questions.Q: How can Phoenix combine tracing and evaluation?
questions.A: Phoenix supports inspecting model-system traces and evaluating behavior using recorded inputs and outputs. It can help connect a quality failure to a particular retrieval, tool, or model span. It is a proposed observability/evaluation alternative here, not an existing backend integration.
questions.Why: Use safe trace recording to connect failures with evaluation feedback. Review deployment, exporters, retention, and dataset identity rather than adopting a platform for its interface alone.
questions.Risk: Automatic instrumentation may capture sensitive arguments or create duplicate spans alongside LangSmith. Local hosting alone does not guarantee safe access control or retention.
questions.Trade: Correlated traces and evaluation improve diagnosis but require export policy, span conventions, and service operation. One well-configured backend is often enough.
questions.Try: Define the minimum trace fields needed to explain a wrong policy answer, then compare that allowlist with an automatic export's actual payload.

questions.Q: Where does Promptfoo fit compared with a Python evaluation harness?
questions.A: Promptfoo provides configuration-driven evaluations and assertions over model or application outputs, useful for comparing prompts, providers, and adversarial cases. A Python harness is often more natural for inspecting internal service and database state.
questions.Why: Use configuration-driven providers and assertions for repeatable comparisons. Separate deterministic schema or policy checks from model-judged language criteria and control live side effects.
questions.Risk: A contains assertion can pass on quoted or negated text, and a model-graded assertion still depends on judge quality. End-to-end outputs alone cannot reveal every unsafe intermediate tool call.
questions.Trade: Declarative matrices make broad experiments convenient; custom Python gives finer control over stateful workflows and failure injection.
questions.Try: Define deterministic assertions for an empty result and missing confirmation, then add a reviewed rubric for coverage faithfulness. Explain which checks need backend instrumentation.

questions.Q: How do you make evaluation results comparable across libraries?
questions.A: Preserve a shared case identity, corpus revision, policy applicability, model and prompt identity, exact evidence, trajectory, answer_source, judge configuration, and failure policy. Record raw results before converting them to a common report.
questions.Why: Align task fixtures, inputs, rubric, judge, sampling, thresholds, and versions before comparing scores. Identical metric names can represent different scales and decision rules.
questions.Risk: Averaging one library's probability-like score with another's binary verdict produces an uninterpretable number. Silent skipping of failed cases can also inflate averages.
questions.Trade: Rich records cost storage and support reproducibility. A compact dashboard is useful only when links expose the underlying definitions and examples.
questions.Try: Run the same two synthetic cases through two adapters and compare case coverage, inputs, judge settings, and failure handling before comparing scores.

questions.Q: What evaluation stack is a sensible starting point for this reference design?
questions.A: Retain deterministic pytest contracts for security and writes, use the existing the retrieval service harness for retrieval diagnosis, and add a small opt-in agent trajectory suite. Choose one experiment and tracing workflow, then add one specialized evaluator only for a demonstrated gap.
questions.Why: Start with service invariants, a small agent trajectory suite, and one coherent experiment workflow. Add a new evaluator only for a specific unanswered measurement need.
questions.Risk: Tool proliferation fragments datasets, duplicates provider spend, and increases private-data copies. A simpler stack with reviewed gold cases can produce more reliable engineering decisions.
questions.Trade: Incremental adoption delays some advanced features and keeps failure attribution manageable. Expand when the team can name the question the example tools cannot answer.
questions.Try: Write a one-page evaluation architecture with test tiers, dataset owner, judge budget, privacy policy, and release blockers. Limit the first implementation to three layers.

title: Agent observability and trace privacy
subtitle: Connect requests, tool outcomes, model spend, and business results.

questions.Q: How do logs, metrics, traces, audit records, and evaluations differ?
questions.A: Logs describe events, metrics aggregate measurements, traces connect causal execution spans, audit records document selected authoritative actions, and evaluations assess behavior against expectations. They can correlate through operation IDs but are not substitutes for one another.
questions.Why: Use metrics for trends, logs for events, traces for causal execution, audit for required accountability, and evaluation for quality. Give each a retention and failure policy suited to its purpose.
questions.Risk: A successful trace export does not prove a business committed, and an audit row does not explain a model's poor retrieval. Confusing these roles produces incomplete incident diagnosis.
questions.Trade: Multiple signals add operational work and answer different questions. Start with a small coherent schema rather than unrelated dashboards.
questions.Try: For a failed confirmation after a successful model turn, state which signal proves the transaction result and which explains the preceding tool choice.

questions.Q: What should a useful agent trace tree contain?
questions.A: One request or turn root should connect relevant model, tool, retrieval, and persistence activity with durations and sanitized outcomes. Include operation and version metadata needed to reproduce the failure, while excluding secrets and unnecessary private content.
questions.Why: Create a task or request root and connect model, retrieval, tool, and persistence spans. Include safe operation and release references without storing unnecessary user content.
questions.Risk: Orphan model spans can hide which user-visible turn incurred cost. Copying entire state into attributes creates a privacy problem and a noisy trace.
questions.Trade: Rich trace structure improves diagnosis but adds instrumentation complexity. Keep high-value boundaries stable and avoid tracing every tiny helper.
questions.Try: Draw the trace tree for coverage review with two tool calls, retrieval, one retry, and final persistence. Mark parallel versus sequential time honestly.

questions.Q: Why does the runtime-to-model tracing bridge need explicit context stitching?
questions.A: Different instrumentation layers may not share the same active trace context. A parent turn recorded by one SDK and a completion recorded by another callback can otherwise appear as unrelated runs. Correlation metadata bridges that boundary.
questions.Why: Propagate trace context through supported async and adapter hooks. Verify parentage and avoid brittle monkey patches unless version-specific tests justify the integration.
questions.Risk: Patching a framework seam is sensitive to dependency changes. A successful import does not prove nesting remains correct after an upgrade, and duplicate callbacks can double recorded usage.
questions.Trade: A localized bridge preserves business-code independence and needs targeted compatibility tests. Provider-native tracing can be simpler but may not connect all application activity.
questions.Try: Assert one root turn with nested tool and model spans before and after repeated startup. Verify parent IDs using synthetic data.

questions.Q: How do you distinguish tool exceptions from business failures in telemetry?
questions.A: Record transport/runtime success separately from domain outcome. A function that returns error='backend unavailable' has executed without raising but did not satisfy the user task. An empty successful search is another distinct outcome.
questions.Why: Record function exceptions and returned business failures separately. A successful function invocation may still mean not found, denied, unavailable, or needs confirmation.
questions.Risk: A dashboard based only on exceptions can report excellent tool reliability while users receive failed searches or validations. Mixing not-found with outages also obscures incident severity.
questions.Trade: Typed outcome categories require consistent tool schemas and provide actionable alerts. Raw exception counts are simple and incomplete.
questions.Try: Add outcome dimensions for completed, empty, validation_rejected, unauthorized, backend_failed, and cancelled. Test each without logging private arguments.

questions.Q: How should token and cost telemetry handle unknown prices?
questions.A: Record observed usage, estimated cost, pricing source, and whether pricing is known. Unknown should not be silently interpreted as free. Compare cost per successful task and per stage rather than only per model request.
questions.Why: Resolve usage and pricing independently, retaining unknown and estimated values explicitly. Compare total cost per completed task, including retries and failed runs, with a known pricing source.
questions.Risk: A zero-cost metric can hide a new provider or unsupported model price. Retries, embedding, and reranking may also be omitted from a narrow generation-only dashboard.
questions.Trade: Detailed accounting adds metadata and improves budget control. Provider invoices remain a reconciliation source rather than assuming local estimates are exact bills.
questions.Try: Send a synthetic unknown-model usage record and verify it is reported as unpriced, not confidently free. Attribute all calls in one successful task.

questions.Q: Why are in-process metrics different from fleet-wide monitoring?
questions.A: Process-local counters and bounded event buffers describe one process since its start. They do not automatically aggregate across replicas, survive restarts, or provide a durable long-term time series. Fleet monitoring requires collection and identity rules.
questions.Why: Aggregate across replicas through an external collection system and stable metric definitions. Process-local counters cannot establish a deployment-wide rate or survive restart by themselves.
questions.Risk: Summing request snapshots repeatedly can double count, and restarting a process can look like a sudden drop in demand. High-cardinality labels such as raw request IDs can overwhelm a metrics backend.
questions.Trade: Local metrics are lightweight and useful for debugging; shared systems add infrastructure and coherent operational visibility.
questions.Try: Run two replicas and restart one. Specify how counters, gauges, and histograms should be exported and queried without inventing fleet totals.

questions.Q: How can trace collection disclose private customer data?
questions.A: Tool arguments, results, prompts, completions, exception strings, and URLs can contain customer or claim information. Tracing a trusted tool does not make its payload safe to export. Data minimization must apply before or at the instrumentation/export boundary.
questions.Why: Apply an allowlist before export, redact necessary payloads, and control access and retention. Review embeddings, transcripts, documents, and identifiers as potential disclosure sources.
questions.Risk: Trace readers or vendors may gain access broader than the product's owner-scoped API permits. Confirmation tokens and source text should not appear by accident in support exports.
questions.Trade: Content-rich traces help reproduce model failures and increase privacy obligations. Prefer sanitized fixtures and reviewed sampled content when necessary.
questions.Try: Inventory actual exported payloads for one synthetic request preparation. Define an allowlist and prove a fake token and private description are absent.

questions.Q: Should tracing failures be allowed to fail business operations?
questions.A: Optional telemetry often uses best-effort failure containment to preserve availability. Mandatory business audit may require a different policy. Decide per signal rather than declaring that every kind of observation may be dropped harmlessly.
questions.Why: Keep optional telemetry failure from blocking business work where the product permits it. Required audit may need transactional delivery or a controlled fail-closed policy instead.
questions.Risk: Silent instrumentation failure can leave an incident undiagnosable. Conversely, blocking every request on a slow telemetry vendor can create an avoidable outage.
questions.Trade: Fail-open telemetry improves availability and needs health signals for lost coverage. Transactional audit or a durable audit outbox increases assurance and operational coupling.
questions.Try: Simulate unavailable tracing and unavailable audit storage separately. Define the expected request, readiness, and alert behavior for each.

questions.Q: What SLOs and alerts are useful for a support assistant?
questions.A: Monitor successful authorized task completion, stream completion, backend failures, indexing lag, oldest pending job age, provider throttling, and cost per completed task. Use freshness and correctness signals alongside request latency.
questions.Why: Define SLOs around useful outcomes, response delay, evidence freshness, and recovery. Alert on sustained user impact and preserve a path from aggregate metrics to safe trace identifiers.
questions.Risk: Alerting only on average HTTP latency misses stuck jobs and quality failures. Sampling can also miss rare severe authorization incidents, which need deterministic denial monitoring and tests.
questions.Trade: More nuanced SLOs require definitions and ownership. A small set linked to concrete user impact is more maintainable than dozens of disconnected thresholds.
questions.Try: Define a stream-success SLO and an indexing-lag SLO, including numerator, denominator, window, and corrective action.

questions.Q: How should observability produce better evaluation cases?
questions.A: Triage a failure trace, minimize and sanitize it, establish the correct outcome with a reviewer, and add a versioned regression case. Keep raw production data access restricted and preserve which failure the new case is intended to catch.
questions.Why: Turn reviewed incidents into redacted reproducible fixtures. Keep task category, configuration lineage, observed failure, and expected invariant while avoiding unnecessary customer-data retention.
questions.Risk: Automatically adding model answers as gold labels reinforces errors. Copying production conversations into broad datasets can violate data-minimization policy.
questions.Trade: Reviewed case creation costs human time and improves relevance. Fully synthetic tests scale cheaply and may miss real ambiguity.
questions.Try: Turn one synthetic wrong-policy trace into a case with expected revision, required tool steps, allowed final outcomes, and a clear privacy review.

title: Evidence applicability and decision boundaries
subtitle: Separate support explanations, contractual applicability, and authoritative decisions.

questions.Q: How does explaining eligibility differ from authorizing a business outcome?
questions.A: An assistant can explain documented eligibility rules and identify missing facts. A binding business outcome requires the authorized process, applicable evidence, and an authoritative recorded decision. Clearly communicate which responsibility the product is performing.
questions.Why: Separate explanation from authority. An assistant can summarize applicable rules; a deterministic service and authorized actor own the actual business transition and approval.
questions.Risk: A fluent answer can sound like approval despite missing personal applicability evidence. Distinguish general rules, verified customer-specific facts, and actual recorded decisions.
questions.Trade: Careful conditional explanations may feel less decisive and preserve the actual authority boundary. Automated adjudication is a separate product requiring substantially stronger domain and governance evidence.
questions.Try: Rewrite three coverage answers to state the supporting clause, material conditions, unresolved facts, and whether an authorized decision has actually occurred.

questions.Q: How should event date, submission date, and rule effective date be handled?
questions.A: Event date concerns when something happened, submission date records when a request was filed, and rule effective dates define version applicability. These are separate facts; do not infer one from another merely to fill a required field.
questions.Why: Store event time, submission time, and rule effective intervals separately. Select the applicable revision explicitly and evaluate timezone and boundary cases rather than guessing a missing date.
questions.Risk: Applying today's policy to an earlier incident can produce an inaccurate answer. Time zones and inclusive/exclusive boundary rules also matter for exact applicability.
questions.Trade: Explicit temporal modeling adds query and validation work. A current-only general FAQ is simpler if the UI honestly limits its scope.
questions.Try: Create incidents before, at, and after a policy-version boundary. Specify the applicable interval rule and the evidence required for each answer.

questions.Q: Why must exclusions and conditions be retrieved alongside a positive coverage clause?
questions.A: A positive clause can be limited by exclusions, definitions, sublimits, deductibles, and factual conditions elsewhere. Retrieving one semantically similar paragraph is not necessarily sufficient to explain applicability.
questions.Why: Retrieve linked exceptions and required conditions alongside a positive clause. Group evidence by applicable revision before answering and abstain when a material qualification is unavailable.
questions.Risk: A faithful summary of an isolated clause can still mislead by omitting a controlling exception. More top-k hits may not solve the problem if the corpus lacks structured relationships.
questions.Trade: Targeted follow-up retrieval or structured links improve completeness and add calls and complexity. Large indiscriminate context increases noise and cost.
questions.Try: Build a case where the positive clause ranks highly but its exclusion is elsewhere. Evaluate whether a follow-up query or section expansion retrieves the missing condition.

questions.Q: Why is a section citation weaker than a revision-aware evidence reference?
questions.A: A section label identifies a human-readable location, but may not uniquely identify source, revision, or exact supporting span. A reproducible reference needs enough identity to retrieve what the user originally saw.
questions.Why: Carry source ID, revision, span, and applicability metadata through assembly and citation. Recheck access when opening a historical source instead of treating an identifier as a permission token.
questions.Risk: A later policy edit can make an old answer unverifiable, and section-only deduplication can collapse distinct sources. A fallback source filename is not evidence of the original document's identity.
questions.Trade: Rich citations add metadata and snapshot retention while enabling verification. Simple labels work for a small sample corpus and should not be overstated.
questions.Try: Create two sources with an identically named section and different terms. Design a stable citation key and bounded source-opening API.

questions.Q: How should OCR, tables, photographs, and attachments extend the support pipeline?
questions.A: Treat each modality as a separate extraction and evidence problem. OCR converts visible text, tables need row-column relationships, and photographs may require a vision model or human review. A file upload alone does not create reliable multimodal reasoning.
questions.Why: Preserve original artifacts, OCR text, layout, and region provenance. Validate fields and tables before indexing, and treat extracted instructions as untrusted source content.
questions.Risk: OCR errors in amounts, dates, or negations can change meaning. Attachments can also contain malware, private third-party data, prompt injection, and oversized payloads.
questions.Trade: Richer inputs improve user access and require scanning, extraction confidence, provenance, storage policy, and review states. Text-only support is narrower and easier to validate.
questions.Try: Design an attachment intake state machine with quarantine, extraction, review, indexing, and rejection. Keep source bytes separate from generated interpretations.

questions.Q: Why should fraud or risk signals not be treated as automatic truth?
questions.A: A statistical risk score is evidence for investigation, not proof that a service requestant is dishonest or that a service request should be denied. Training data, false positives, protected proxies, and changing behavior all affect interpretation.
questions.Why: Treat risk predictions as uncertain inputs with reviewed thresholds and an appeal path. Evaluate false positives and subgroup effects before connecting a signal to consequential decisions.
questions.Risk: Presenting an opaque score as a decision can create harmful unsupported accusations and unreliable automation. It also introduces sensitive-data and model-governance obligations beyond this guide's engineering examples.
questions.Trade: Assisted triage can prioritize workload while requiring calibration, review, and appeal paths. Simple rule-based routing may be more transparent for a small system.
questions.Try: Design a review-only output with supporting observable signals, uncertainty, missing information, and prohibited automatic actions. Do not invent a fraud threshold.

questions.Q: How should deterministic calculations complement generated explanations?
questions.A: Use reviewed deterministic code for exact arithmetic under explicitly selected policy rules, then let generation explain the result and assumptions. A model should not invent a deductible, round a monetary value arbitrarily, or apply an unverified formula.
questions.Why: Use deterministic arithmetic with explicit units, currencies, dates, and reviewed formulas. Let the model explain a verified result rather than inventing or silently altering the calculation.
questions.Risk: Correct arithmetic with the wrong rule or knowledge version is still wrong. Caps, sublimits, depreciation, multiple currencies, and exceptions require domain-approved logic.
questions.Trade: Deterministic calculators improve reproducibility and need versioned business specifications. Free-form arithmetic is convenient and unsuitable as authoritative financial logic.
questions.Try: Write a hypothetical deductible calculation with explicit inputs and rounding, then state which real knowledge facts must be verified before using it.

questions.Q: What should a real human-escalation record contain?
questions.A: Store the originating operation, authorized user or case, reason, minimal evidence, destination, delivery state, and an acknowledgement or failure. Distinguish requested, accepted, in progress, and completed rather than claiming connection from generated prose alone.
questions.Why: Create a durable handoff record with owner, urgency, evidence, completed actions, and unresolved questions. Report actual acceptance state instead of promising human contact without an integration.
questions.Risk: Exporting a full conversation can disclose unnecessary personal data, and a failed handoff can leave a user waiting without an actual owner.
questions.Trade: Structured escalation adds integration work and truthful operational status. A clear support-contact instruction is a legitimate simpler fallback.
questions.Try: Specify a proposed handoff service and acceptance tests for delivery failure, duplicate requests, revoked access, and a later human response.

questions.Q: How should fairness and accessibility be evaluated in customer support?
questions.A: Evaluate whether the assistant handles equivalent requests consistently across language, writing style, disability-related interaction needs, and differing levels of domain knowledge. Focus on support outcomes and access, not unsupported automated judgments about protected traits.
questions.Why: Evaluate realistic language, literacy, disability, and channel variations under reviewed criteria. Report subgroup results and preserve a usable non-voice or human-assisted alternative.
questions.Risk: Simplified wording can accidentally omit a condition, while multilingual retrieval can fail under ASCII lexical fallback. Voice or OCR inputs introduce another representation gap.
questions.Trade: Broader evaluation and interface support cost effort and improve real usability. Clearly bounded supported languages are preferable to an untested universal claim.
questions.Try: Create semantically equivalent questions in plain language, formal wording, and a supported second language. Compare evidence, clarification, and escalation outcomes.

questions.Q: How should the application explain uncertainty without hiding system failure?
questions.A: Explain whether facts are missing, evidence is absent, the source is inapplicable, or a backend is unavailable. Give the strongest supported statement while preserving a distinct failure status. Uncertainty should guide the next action rather than be a vague disclaimer appended to everything.
questions.Why: Return typed missing-input, insufficient-evidence, conflict, and unavailable states. Explain the next useful step without presenting an infrastructure failure as proof that no relevant record exists.
questions.Risk: An outage can be mistaken for proof that the policy says nothing. Reassuring language may also imply a specialist handoff that never happened.
questions.Trade: Explicit statuses require API and UI changes but make retries and support decisions honest. Text-only fallback is simple and ambiguous.
questions.Try: Design separate responses for missing incident facts, no matching clause, source outage, stale policy, and completed escalation. Map each to a testable backend status.

title: Full-stack streaming and user workflows
subtitle: Carry backend truth into browser state, confirmation, and feedback.

questions.Q: What is the public SSE contract, and why should the browser not parse raw ADK internals?
questions.A: The API maps runtime events into text_delta, tool_call, tool_result, tool_error, error, and response_complete messages. A stable application contract lets the UI evolve independently of ADK and supports a future orchestrator adapter.
questions.Why: Map provider or framework events into a versioned public contract. Persist the answer before exposing its final message ID and keep internal tool arguments out of the public stream.
questions.Risk: Forwarding raw runtime objects can leak fields and break the UI after dependency changes. A stream ending at the network layer is not necessarily a successful response_complete event.
questions.Trade: An adapter adds code and preserves product stability. Direct runtime streaming is quicker for a demo and creates tighter coupling.
questions.Try: Capture a synthetic successful and failed stream. Verify event discriminators, JSON validity, and exactly one meaningful terminal outcome for the actual route path.

questions.Q: How should a browser parse streaming chunks correctly?
questions.A: Buffer bytes across network reads, decode incrementally, split complete SSE frames, parse their JSON, and retain any unfinished suffix. A network chunk may contain half a JSON object or several events; it is not an event boundary.
questions.Why: Decode UTF-8 incrementally and accumulate SSE fields through the blank-line delimiter. Validate the completed event payload separately and test every relevant network fragmentation boundary.
questions.Risk: Naive JSON.parse on each read loses events or fails on multibyte characters. Error recovery must also distinguish a malformed event from a clean terminal completion.
questions.Trade: A small parser handles a narrow contract; a mature SSE client can cover more protocol details. Test the actual API framing and reconnection requirements.
questions.Try: Feed the same stream split at every possible byte boundary, including inside Unicode text. Verify identical parsed events.

questions.Q: Why do persisted message IDs matter for feedback?
questions.A: Feedback should reference an actual assistant message owned by the user, not a temporary browser-generated ID. The backend can then authorize the record and connect a rating to its conversation, evidence, model configuration, and trace.
questions.Why: Bind feedback to an owner-scoped persisted answer or operation. A client-supplied message ID must not allow another user to label or retrieve private conversation data.
questions.Risk: Rating an optimistic local ID can fail or attach feedback to the wrong turn. A persistence failure may leave partial text visible but no authoritative message to rate.
questions.Trade: Waiting for server identity adds a final synchronization step and preserves referential integrity. Client-only messages are easy to render and weak as durable references.
questions.Try: Simulate a stream that generates text but fails persistence. Define whether feedback is disabled and how retry behaves without duplicating the displayed answer.

questions.Q: What should the UI state machine distinguish during a turn?
questions.A: Distinguish draft, accepted, searching or tooling, generating, completed, failed, cancelled, and disconnected. Track evidence and persistence status separately where needed. A spinner stopping is not proof that the model completed successfully.
questions.Why: Use explicit waiting, running, streaming, review, complete, incomplete, failed, and cancelled states. Transitions should follow typed outcomes rather than the presence of some generated text.
questions.Risk: Treating every closed connection as completion can show truncated service requests as final. Late responses from a prior conversation or signed-out user can also contaminate current state.
questions.Trade: Explicit states add frontend logic and improve recovery. A single loading boolean is compact and cannot represent the important distinctions.
questions.Try: Create a reducer for stream events and test disconnect before completion, tool failure, persistence failure, cancellation, and a late event after tenant or conversation change.

questions.Q: How should request confirmation be presented and protected in the UI?
