questions.A: Display the exact prepared fields, identify that no claim is yet submitted, and send the token through the authenticated confirmation route only after the user's action. Disable duplicate controls for usability while retaining server-side race protection.
questions.Why: Present exact parameters, operation identity, expiry, and revision. Disable misleading repeated actions in the UI, but rely on server-side approval validation and transactional idempotency for correctness.
questions.Risk: Corrections can leave old pending tokens valid unless the server supersedes them. The UI must not promise revocation that only exists in prompt text.
questions.Trade: A review screen adds friction and supports consent to material fields. The authoritative check must remain on the server because browsers can retry or be bypassed.
questions.Try: Test double click, refresh, expired token, cancellation race, and correction after preparation. Compare displayed state with the actual submission record.

questions.Q: How should browser caching respond to sign-out, role changes, and archived conversations?
questions.A: Partition cached results by trusted user and relevant resource identity, cancel or ignore obsolete in-flight responses, and clear private state at sign-out. Revalidate permissions for source opening and mutation even if a cached view once allowed access.
questions.Why: Invalidate or partition client caches by authenticated identity and permission revision. Cancel streams and clear private view state on sign-out, while retaining server-side ownership checks on every fetch.
questions.Risk: Reusing query keys across users can show private content without making a new unauthorized request. Hidden or archived messages can also remain in model context unless their lifecycle is mapped deliberately.
questions.Trade: Aggressive invalidation costs network requests and preserves clear session boundaries. Long-lived caches improve responsiveness and need stronger partitioning and freshness rules.
questions.Try: Switch users during a slow stream and verify no old message, source, or confirmation token appears in the new user's interface.

questions.Q: How should citations and tool activity be rendered accessibly and safely?
questions.A: Render untrusted text safely, expose expandable source details by keyboard, use meaningful labels, and avoid announcing every token to assistive technology. Show user-relevant activity without exposing internal prompts, private tool arguments, or raw exception data.
questions.Why: Render model text as text or a sanitized approved subset. Validate links and avoid treating returned HTML or tool output as trusted application markup.
questions.Risk: Raw HTML or unsafe URLs can create XSS, and a busy live region can make streaming unusable. A similarity distance should not be displayed as percent certainty.
questions.Trade: Progressive disclosure reduces overload but must keep verification discoverable. Detailed internal traces belong in authorized operator tools, not the customer screen.
questions.Try: Review a synthetic answer using only the keyboard and a screen reader. Include malicious markup and long source titles in the fixture.

questions.Q: How should client retries preserve operation identity?
questions.A: Reuse one idempotency key for retries of the same logical request, but create a new operation for a genuinely changed request. Record whether the server accepted or completed it. Claim confirmation should rely on its own token and durable state, not a generic chat response cache.
questions.Why: Preserve a durable operation key across retries and distinguish request deduplication from business idempotency. After an uncertain outcome, query status rather than restarting a write blindly.
questions.Risk: Reusing a key with a changed body should fail rather than replay another answer. Retrying a long-running request after a best-effort Redis wait can still duplicate model calls.
questions.Trade: Explicit operation identity requires lifecycle handling and supports predictable retries. Automatically retrying all failures is easy and can repeat expensive work.
questions.Try: Test same key/same body, same key/changed body, new key/same body, and an ambiguous timeout. Document behavior for chat versus confirmation.

questions.Q: How should frontend, API, and agent contracts be tested together?
questions.A: Use a small set of full user journeys plus focused contract tests for events, ownership, persistence IDs, and confirmation effects. Fake providers make UI tests deterministic; separate live-provider tests assess actual model behavior.
questions.Why: Expose a stable API error and outcome schema across frontend and backend. Version incompatible changes and test clients against missing, delayed, duplicate, and unknown event types.
questions.Risk: A mocked stream that always ends successfully cannot reveal cancellation or malformed-event behavior. Live model tests alone are too variable for every UI assertion.
questions.Trade: Layered tests provide fast diagnosis and credible integration coverage. Excessive end-to-end duplication raises cost without necessarily testing new behavior.
questions.Try: Define five journeys: cited answer, corrected preparation, denied foreign claim, failed stream, and post-restart history. State the provider and database realism each needs.

questions.Q: What should the completed portfolio demonstration show?
questions.A: Show one coherent user journey across authentication, evidence retrieval, streaming, source verification, request preparation, confirmation, background indexing, and feedback. Then demonstrate a denial and a recovery case with supporting traces and tests.
questions.Why: Demonstrate identity, evidence, approved effects, cancellation, restart recovery, and quality measurement in one coherent journey. Use synthetic data and show a failure as well as success.
questions.Risk: A polished recording can hide unimplemented handoff, current-only policy scope, or in-memory deployment state. State those limitations and show the effective configuration.
questions.Trade: A narrow reliable application is more persuasive than many unverified agent features. Add remote agents or model adaptation only when the measured problem justifies them.
questions.Try: Prepare a ten-minute demo with architecture, one successful task, one adversarial denial, one crash recovery, and a held-out quality/cost report.

title: Deployment, recovery, and production readiness
subtitle: Turn local mechanisms into a measured deployment contract.

questions.Q: What must change when scaling from one process to multiple replicas?
questions.A: Shared sessions, idempotency, rate limits, jobs, migrations, and telemetry need explicit cross-process semantics. Process-local dictionaries, locks, and counters remain local even when replicas run identical code.
questions.Why: Move authoritative tasks, sessions, rate accounting, and operation identity into deliberately shared stores where required. Test concurrent replicas instead of extrapolating from one process.
questions.Risk: Adding replicas can multiply quotas, repeat model calls, and split conversational state. A load balancer does not make local state shared.
questions.Trade: Shared services improve continuity and introduce network dependencies. One process with honest limitations can be a simpler initial deployment.
questions.Try: Test retries routed to another replica, session continuation, worker claiming, and global quota behavior during Redis failure.

questions.Q: Should migrations run on every application startup?
questions.A: Startup migration is convenient for small deployments but couples readiness to schema changes and can make replicas compete to migrate. A controlled migration job followed by compatible application rollout is an alternative.
questions.Why: Give one deployment step ownership of reviewed migrations and deploy compatible application versions. Define upgrade failure and rollback behavior before enabling multiple startup processes.
questions.Risk: Concurrent DDL, long locks, and destructive changes can affect all replicas. A schema change can also prevent rollback to the prior image.
questions.Trade: Self-initializing services reduce manual steps; dedicated migration stages improve sequencing. Either requires tested failure behavior and appropriate database privileges.
questions.Try: Design a rolling deployment with one migrator, compatible schema, application rollout, verification, and delayed cleanup.

questions.Q: Why does startup ingestion need separate operational treatment?
questions.A: Ingestion performs provider calls and writes unrelated to accepting a web request. Running it during every replica startup can duplicate preparation, delay readiness, and couple scaling to source and model availability.
questions.Why: Run ingestion as a versioned background workflow with freshness state, deduplication, deadlines, and retry policy. Avoid repeating expensive source preparation on each replica startup.
questions.Risk: A service can start successfully with missing knowledge. Database connectivity does not prove usable policy evidence exists.
questions.Trade: Startup ingestion suits a sample corpus; a scheduled or operator-triggered worker gives clearer ownership, progress, and recovery.
questions.Try: Start two replicas with an unchanged source, then with an unavailable provider. Report effective readiness, freshness, and duplicate preparation.

questions.Q: What does the minimal health endpoint prove?
questions.A: A bounded database probe establishes only that a basic connection and query worked at that moment. It does not prove model availability, current evidence, healthy workers, correct permissions, or functioning event delivery.
questions.Why: Separate process liveness, dependency readiness, index freshness, and task-quality signals. Bound probes and avoid costly model calls on every health check.
questions.Risk: Calling this fully healthy can conceal an assistant unable to answer or index. Putting expensive evaluations in every probe can instead overload the service.
questions.Trade: Cheap probes suit frequent checks. Readiness and scheduled consistency checks should cover critical product dependencies separately.
questions.Try: Define probe outcomes for database failure, provider failure, stale corpus, and a stopped embedding worker.

questions.Q: How should connection pools and worker concurrency be sized together?
questions.A: Count API requests, background jobs, agent-session writes, migrations, and probes that need connections. Bound concurrency and pool waits so one workload cannot consume all capacity. Async I/O does not remove database connection limits.
questions.Why: Multiply pool limits by processes and replicas, then reserve database headroom for workers and operations. Bound simultaneous queries separately from model or HTTP concurrency.
questions.Risk: Increasing replicas can exceed the total connection budget. Provider waits inside open transactions amplify occupancy even when CPU usage is low.
questions.Trade: Larger pools reduce local waiting until database saturation; smaller pools protect the database and need admission control.
questions.Try: Calculate connections across replicas and workers, reserve operational headroom, and measure pool checkout latency under load.

questions.Q: How should container and dependency hardening be evaluated?
questions.A: Review non-root execution, image contents, dependency resolution, vulnerability handling, secrets, and runtime privileges. A production filename or non-root USER is one control rather than complete supply-chain assurance.
questions.Why: Review base images, non-root execution, dependency resolution, runtime packages, and artifact provenance. Exact direct pins alone do not establish a reproducible environment or safe deployment.
questions.Risk: Without constrained resolution and compatibility checks, upgrades can break ADK events, tracing patches, or provider behavior. Build tools and unnecessary files also add maintenance surface.
questions.Trade: Strict locking improves repeatability and requires planned updates. Broad ranges support experimentation and weaken deployment reproducibility.
questions.Try: Compare resolved dependencies from two clean builds and propose a tested update policy without changing the support repository.

questions.Q: How should worker shutdown and stale-job recovery be verified?
questions.A: Stop accepting new work, allow bounded completion, release resources, and use durable job state for later recovery. A finally block helps graceful shutdown but cannot be guaranteed after abrupt process death.
questions.Why: Stop accepting new work, allow or cancel active operations under a deadline, persist state, and recover stale leases safely. Verify shutdown through controlled worker interruption.
questions.Risk: Reclaiming too early overlaps workers; never reclaiming strands jobs. A crash after external delivery but before completion marking can repeat delivery.
questions.Trade: Graceful draining improves continuity and slows replacement. Abrupt replacement is faster and demands stronger recovery invariants.
questions.Try: Terminate a worker after claim, after embedding, and after delivery. Verify the next worker converges without duplicate logical effects.

questions.Q: How should an external provider outage affect the product?
questions.A: Distinguish unavailable generation, unavailable embeddings, failed retrieval, and degraded tracing. Preserve committed business state and expose retryable status. Do not fabricate policy answers or report unperformed actions as successful.
questions.Why: Classify affected capabilities and provide explicit degraded outcomes. Apply bounded retries and circuit or admission policies without generating unsupported answers when evidence or tools are unavailable.
questions.Risk: Nested retries can exhaust pools and budgets. Switching providers can change tool and privacy behavior and must be an explicit evaluated policy.
questions.Trade: Structured status lookup can preserve useful service while generation is unavailable. Full-availability service requests are inappropriate when essential evidence is missing.
questions.Try: Define an outage matrix for PostgreSQL, Redis, embedding, generation, and tracing, with permitted operations and recovery behavior.

questions.Q: What is a meaningful disaster-recovery drill?
questions.A: Restore authoritative data, recover or rebuild derived indexes, reconcile jobs, validate ownership, and demonstrate post-restart application behavior. Measure actual recovery time and data loss against declared objectives.
questions.Why: Restore a known fixture and reconcile authoritative records, outbox state, indexes, and access policy. Measure actual recovery duration and data-loss exposure rather than relying on backup existence.
questions.Risk: Old jobs may replay and stale vectors may remain visible. Backups themselves also need secure access, retention, and credential-restoration procedures.
questions.Trade: Frequent drills cost effort and reveal dependencies that documents miss. Backup configuration alone is not proof of recoverability.
questions.Try: Restore a fixture with a service request, pending job, rule revision, and archived conversation. Produce a reconciliation report.

questions.Q: What evidence supports a production-readiness claim?
questions.A: Show effective configuration, tested authorization and transaction boundaries, migration ownership, restore evidence, queue and latency measurements, quality limits, privacy policy, and incident ownership. State the workload and scope under which the service request holds.
questions.Why: Collect deployment-specific evidence for invariants, capacity, recovery, security, and quality. Document limits honestly and retain rollback; a container build or green process probe is only one check.
questions.Risk: A polished architecture or passing unit suite can conceal untested runtime behavior. Secure, scalable, and exactly once are service requests requiring specific evidence.
questions.Trade: Readiness work is slower than a demo and establishes a defensible operational contract. A prototype may ship earlier with narrower commitments.
questions.Try: Assemble a release packet with concurrency results, quality report, dependency inventory, privacy review, restore drill, and rollback plan.

title: Model engineering and the advanced learning path
subtitle: Connect representation, uncertainty, serving, and experimentation to actual failures.

questions.Q: What mathematical foundations should an AI full-stack engineer learn first?
questions.A: Learn vectors, norms, dot products, probability, conditional probability, cross-entropy, optimization, and basic statistics. Connect them to retrieval geometry, training, calibration, and evaluation rather than memorizing formulas without a system consequence.
questions.Why: Practice vector arithmetic, dot products, probability, gradients, and optimization with small executable examples. Connect each operation to embeddings, attention, training objectives, and inference instead of memorizing terms alone.
questions.Risk: A number can look authoritative while measuring the wrong event. Similarity is not truth probability, and judge agreement is not calibrated decision confidence.
questions.Trade: API skills enable quick prototypes; foundations improve diagnosis. Alternate practical exercises with theory.
questions.Try: Compute normalized similarity by hand and estimate uncertainty in a small benchmark. Explain what each number establishes.

questions.Q: How do calibration and selective answering differ from ranking?
questions.A: Ranking orders candidates; calibration relates predicted confidence to observed correctness; selective answering chooses when to abstain. Define correctness and harm before turning a score into a decision threshold.
questions.Why: Define correctness and error cost, calibrate scores on reviewed outcomes, and report accuracy alongside answer coverage. A high ranking score is not automatically a confidence probability.
questions.Risk: A threshold tuned only on answerable questions can accept unsupported claims. Rare severe errors require separate treatment from average accuracy.
questions.Trade: More abstention can improve reliability among answered cases while reducing coverage. Evaluate the risk-coverage relationship with reviewed labels.
questions.Try: Plot answered fraction against error rate across candidate thresholds. Separate outages, missing facts, and inapplicable knowledge rules.

questions.Q: What are hard negatives and why can domain retrieval need them?
questions.A: Hard negatives appear relevant but fail a material condition, such as gradual leakage versus a sudden burst. They test whether representation and reranking distinguish the condition the user's question depends on.
questions.Why: Use reviewed non-relevant examples that resemble the query to teach finer distinctions. Keep false negatives out of training and compare retrieval improvements on held-out domain tasks.
questions.Risk: Binary labels can incorrectly mark a controlling exclusion irrelevant. Distinguish supporting, contradicting, conditional, and unrelated evidence when the task requires it.
questions.Trade: Rich labels cost review effort and reveal meaningful limitations. Easy random negatives produce cheaper and often flattering scores.
questions.Try: Build a query with a positive clause, exclusion, unrelated clause, and ambiguous condition. Evaluate candidate recall and evidence completeness separately.

questions.Q: When should you adapt an embedding or reranker instead of changing the prompt?
questions.A: Adapt representation when evidence consistently fails candidate retrieval or ranking after extraction, chunking, and labeling are correct. Change answer policy when useful evidence arrives but generation ignores it or overservice requests.
questions.Why: Improve representation or ranking when the correct evidence consistently fails candidate recall or relevance ordering. Tune prompts when evidence is already correct and generation misuses it; evaluate each failure separately.
questions.Risk: Tiny-domain tuning can overfit visible questions and worsen rare exclusions or other languages. Training leakage can conceal the regression.
questions.Trade: Adaptation may improve difficult matching and adds training and migration cost. Structured metadata or deterministic routing can be cheaper.
questions.Try: Classify twenty failures by the first stage losing correctness and justify adaptation only after simpler repairs fail.

questions.Q: What do distillation and synthetic data add to a learning plan?
questions.A: Distillation trains a smaller system from a stronger teacher's signals. Synthetic data expands examples, paraphrases, or adversarial cases. Both require independent validation because confident teacher errors can be copied at scale.
questions.Why: Distillation transfers behavior from a stronger teacher under a defined objective. Synthetic data can broaden fixtures or training examples, but needs validation, diversity checks, provenance, and separation from held-out evaluation.
questions.Risk: Generated questions can mirror source wording and overstate generalization. Generated answers should not become gold labels without review.
questions.Trade: Synthetic expansion reduces annotation effort and can reduce diversity or amplify bias. Keep a reviewed core as the anchor.
questions.Try: Generate toy paraphrases, review them, and compare held-out quality before and after using the accepted data.

questions.Q: How do quantization, batching, and caching affect serving differently?
questions.A: Quantization changes numerical precision, batching groups execution, and caching reuses prior results under a valid identity. They optimize different costs and can change quality, waiting latency, privacy, and freshness differently.
questions.Why: Measure quantization, batching, caching, and serving concurrency on representative hardware and tasks. Report quality, throughput, tail latency, and memory together.
questions.Risk: Cached answers may be stale after policy or permission changes. Aggressive batching can delay interactive requests, and quantization may change task quality.
questions.Trade: Optimizations reduce resources and add operational complexity. Measure successful task cost and tail latency rather than throughput alone.
questions.Try: List what each optimization changes or reuses, its invalidation identity, and the quality tests it requires.

questions.Q: Why separate model quality from inference-system reliability?
questions.A: A capable model can fail through timeouts, rate limits, broken schemas, streaming errors, or unsupported settings. A reliable serving path can consistently deliver poor reasoning. Measure execution availability and behavioral quality separately.
questions.Why: Separate inference, tool, retrieval, queue, and network costs. Provider sampling settings and context size affect both quality and operational behavior, so version them with experiments.
questions.Risk: Replacing a model to fix a parser or transaction bug wastes effort and can introduce incompatibilities. More retries cannot repair consistently unsupported reasoning.
questions.Trade: Layered measurement requires instrumentation and identifies effective changes. One end-to-end score captures impact but does not locate cause.
questions.Try: Create incidents in model, retrieval, tool, transport, database, and frontend categories. State which signal identifies each.

questions.Q: How should experimentation record lineage and reproducibility?
questions.A: Record code and dependency revisions, corpus, source versions, chunking, profiles, prompts, generation settings, judge configuration, and execution mode. Keep case identity stable without assuming temporary chunk UUIDs never change.
questions.Why: Store model, prompt, context, data, code, and environment identifiers with measured outputs. Distinguish configured, observed, estimated, and unknown values in reports.
questions.Risk: Equal model names may hide provider changes. Broad dependency ranges or a context-proxy fallback can change metrics without an obvious application diff.
questions.Trade: Rich lineage costs metadata and supports meaningful comparison. A screenshot of one average is easier to share and cannot reproduce a result.
questions.Try: Write a machine-readable experiment manifest distinguishing configured, observed, estimated, and unknown values.

questions.Q: What advanced topics should follow the core journey?
questions.A: Study temporal retrieval, reranker training, calibration, multimodal extraction, secure workflow persistence, distributed agent tasks, serving economics, privacy-aware evaluation, and failure-oriented operations. Add each through a concrete benchmark or product need.
questions.Why: Choose advanced topics from measured weaknesses: multilingual retrieval, model adaptation, efficient serving, multimodal grounding, privacy, fairness, or distributed agent recovery. Run controlled experiments rather than adding every available framework.
questions.Risk: Collecting techniques without mastering ownership, transactions, and evidence creates complexity with weak guarantees. Reading an API tutorial is not operational experience.
questions.Trade: Deep understanding of complete workflows builds judgment; broad exploration is useful when tied to falsifiable experiments.
questions.Try: Pick one advanced track and define prerequisites, a toy experiment, a held-out metric, a failure test, and a stopping condition.

questions.Q: What demonstrates completion of the full AI full-stack learning journey?
questions.A: Build and explain the path from source bytes to authorized evidence, conversational intent to validated tools, reviewed action to atomic commit, and measured behavior to deployment and recovery. Defend alternatives with observations rather than slogans.
questions.Why: Show an end-to-end application, evaluated outcomes, failure recovery, and defended decisions. Completion is demonstrated engineering ability rather than finishing a list of technology names.
questions.Risk: Familiarity from reading can exceed practical skill. Production service requests need real integration, security, load, and recovery evidence beyond static review.
questions.Trade: A sustained portfolio is slower than memorization and stronger evidence of competence. Finish one reliable product before adding orchestration layers.
questions.Try: Deliver the capstone with a working assistant, held-out report, write tests, trace-privacy review, restore drill, and three defended architectural alternatives.
